docs.lead_paragraph: India’s population has grown to 1.21 billion, second to only China, according to new census data. And despite a decade of slower population growth — it was 17.6 percent from 2001-2011, down from 21.5 percent in the 10 years before that — India still gained 181 million new people over that period, roughly the entire population of Pakistan. The government’s efforts to improve conditions for Indian women seemed to be borne out in some of the data, including an increase in female literacy that was higher than the country’s overall improvement, up about 9 percent to a nationwide literacy rate of 74 percent. But Indian officials expressed alarm about one statistic: the ratio of young girls to young boys (counting those 6 years or younger) fell over the past 10 years, from 927 girls per 1,000 boys in 2001 to 914 per 1,000 in 2011. That raised worries that despite laws to prohibit it, many families are still using abortion to ensure that they have sons.

headline.main: India: To 1.21 Billion, but More Slowly

docs.abstract: The forgotten story of three “contrabands,” a pragmatic general and a shrug that made history.
docs.snippet: The forgotten story of three “contrabands,” a pragmatic general and a shrug that made history.
docs.lead_paragraph: On May 23, 1861, little more than a month into the Civil War, three young black men rowed across the James River in Virginia and claimed asylum in a Union-held citadel. Fort Monroe, Va., a fishhook-shaped spit of land near the mouth of the Chesapeake Bay, had been a military post since the time of the first Jamestown settlers. This spot where the slaves took refuge was also, by remarkable coincidence, the spot where slavery first took root, one summer day in 1619, when a Dutch ship landed with some 20 African captives for the fledgling Virginia Colony.

headline.main: How Slavery Really Ended in America
headline.print_headline: THE SHRUG THAT MADE HISTORY

docs.lead_paragraph: My first daughter was only 2 when I learned I was having twins, and so I still remembered clearly how giddy people were when I was pregnant with her. They’d gleefully tell me tales of 30-hour labors, leaky bladders, struggling marriages. Not so with multiples. From the beginning, people reacted badly to the news. It was as if I had the plague and were coughing in their living room. One friend was openly angry. Some wanted to know exactly what to do to avoid this happening to them. Others just wrinkled their noses as if I’d stepped into a dog-deposited mess. “No,” they said. “Really?”

docs.lead_paragraph: It’s unclear why Jim Shepard tends to collect his short stories under titles that seem more like shrugs: his latest, “You Think That’s Bad,” follows a 2007 volume called “Like You’d Understand, Anyway.” The contents are anything but lackadaisical. Shepard’s taut, high-­concept, research-dependent fiction covers a bracing, career-long range of hobbyhorses and obsessions. Nazis, horror movies, aircraft and explorers abound. Historical fiction is typically so ample and epilogic that the “historical short story” may seem a contradiction in terms, but Shepard has made himself, in particular, a master of this small, tricky subgenre. (His colleague at Williams College, Andrea Barrett, is another.)

headline.main: Jim Shepard, Master of the Historical Short Story

Among the food vendors making a debut are Brooklyn Bangers, a sausage-sandwich concept from Saul Bolton, the chef of Saul and the Vanderbilt, and Fany Gerson’s Dough, where a variety of her doughnuts with hot chocolate will be sold on both days. Christina Tosi from Momofuku Milk Bar also joins the mix with sweets like grapefruit and hibiscus jam. Oystergirl, from the folks behind Mary’s Fish Camp, will shuck oysters, for $1.50 to $3 each, Saturday only. The Kings County Jerky stand and pies from Rachel’s Pies will also operate on Saturdays. The new Sunday-only vendors at the waterfront include Sam Mason’s Empire Mayonnaise, where he will debut artisanal-made mayonnaise served with fries; organic handmade pastas from Rochester, N.Y.-based Flour City Pasta; sweet and savory Czech-style pastry pies from Frgal; smoked meats from Mile End; sandwiches from Saltie and various soups from Sea Bean Goods. Over the past 17 years, he’s written 11 novels — we’ll turn to the 12th in a moment — as remarkable for their precise, economical language and depth of characterization as for the fact that each is as different from its predecessor, in style, tone and narrative approach, as if it had come from a different author.

docs.lead_paragraph: In his testimony on Capitol Hill yesterday, Secretary of Defense Robert Gates made what amounted to an eloquent, even impassioned case against United States involvement in Libya. He highlighted the weakness of the rebel forces: Calling them an opposition is “a misnomer,” he suggested, describing the rebels as “very disparate, very scattered,” “lacking command and control and lacking organization,” and “pretty much a pickup ballgame at this point.” Their “governance capacity” for a post-Qaddafi Libya, he added, is “limited, if not nonexistent.” He put great stress on America’s pre-existing commitments: “I am preoccupied with avoiding mission creep, avoiding an open-ended, very large scale commitment in this respect … The last thing this country needs is another exercise in nationbuilding.” And he basically threatened to resign if the White House somehow decided to send ground forces into Libya: “Not as long as I’m in this job,” he said, when asked about the possibility of putting (non-C.I.A.) boots on the ground.

Doctorow’s greatest triumphs — Doctorow is familiar more by reputation than by any direct influence. Certainly we’ve heard of him; probably every college-educated, newspaper-­reading person in America has heard of him, and has a vague sense that he is, as his press kit puts it, “Ameri­ca’s Pre-­eminent Novelist.” But what kind of novelist? And what does his considerable body of work — 11 novels and more awards than you can count on one hand — represent? Judging from my own experience and that of my peers, a generation later his literary descendants haven’t gotten the memo.

docs.snippet: James McMullan — whose illustrations were the visual inspiration for “Saturday Night Fever” — is now known for the elegantly expressive show posters he makes for Lincoln Center Theater; this week a large selection of those posters have gone on dis...
docs.lead_paragraph: Parents of small children probably know James McMullan as the creator (along with his wife, Kate) of the popular picture book “I Stink!” about the nightly rounds of a profoundly disgusting but hard-working New York City garbage truck. He is also enshrined in disco lore for the paintings he did more than 30 years ago for New York magazine that became the visual inspiration for “Saturday Night Fever.” But these days Mr. McMullan is much better known for the elegantly expressive show posters he makes for Lincoln Center Theater. And this week a large selection of those posters – for plays and musicals like “Ah! Wilderness,” “Carousel” and “South Pacific” – went on display near the theater they helped promote, at the New York Public Library for the Performing Arts, on Lincoln Center Plaza off Amsterdam Avenue near 64th Street. The posters, as well as preliminary sketches, photographs and watercolor and gouache studies, will remain on view at the library through June 11, and on April 4, Mr. McMullan will join fellow theatrical graphic artist Frank Verlizzo, known as Fraver, at the library for a discussion about the living art of poster-making.

headline.main: The Illustrator of ‘I Stink!’ Shows Off his More Elegant Work

Feynman, which ensued after his death in 1988, a publishing entrepreneur might have been tempted to start a book club of works by and about him. docs.lead_paragraph: It’s not easy for a refugee to retain his dignity, nor is it necessarily a goal. Like a hermit crab that has outgrown its shell, a refugee must seize the best shelter he can before another needy creature is able to grab it. Nevertheless, in David Bezmozgis’s first novel, “The Free World,” set in Rome in 1978, a proud Soviet Jewish émigré couple, seeking visas, take offense when a clerk in the briefing department asks for their “Persecution Story.” “What do we need this for?” the wife asks. “Nobody’s saying you need it,” the clerk explains. “The Americans need it. You’re claiming refugee status. To be a refugee you need to have been persecuted.” To which the wife indignantly retorts: “The entire country was persecuted.”

docs.abstract: The Australian poet Les Murray offers a memoir of his depression, and a new book of verse.
docs.snippet: The Australian poet Les Murray offers a memoir of his depression, and a new book of verse.
docs.lead_paragraph: The signature quality of a Les Murray poem is anger — a visceral smoldering that freshly lights up the tired old landscape and turns conventional pieties inside out. A lifelong outsider and champion of the underdog, Murray grew up among impoverished farmers in rural Australia, where, as an overweight “redneck” teenager, he was mercilessly tormented at school. Today he is the closest thing Australia has to a national poet. A sui generis autodidact (he now suspects he has Asperger’s syndrome) equipped with a fierce moral vision and a sensuous musicality, he writes subtly about post­colonialism, urban sprawl and poverty and, in his most intimate poems, reminds us of the power of literature to transubstantiate grievance into insight. (His admirers have argued he ought to be considered for a Nobel.) But he is equally capable of writing emotionally simplistic and strangely soured poems in which the enraged adolescent emerges all but unmediated. This mercurial doubleness can make his work hard to categorize or describe: this is a mind at once revolutionary and reactionary. Or maybe just a poet who’s willing to show more id than most.

headline.main: Les Murray and the Poetry of Depression
headline.print_headline: The Angry Muse

docs.lead_paragraph: Military victory — to adapt Oscar Wilde — is rarely pure and never simple. The Allied triumph in Europe at the end of World War II was a case in point. The war and the Holocaust forced millions of civilians across national frontiers. Afterward, multitudes of ethnic Germans were expelled from Eastern Europe and many of the Jews in Poland fled from a new wave of persecution there. Those lucky enough to survive these migrations faced months and years in limbo as the authorities wrestled with the logistical, political and moral difficulties involved in returning them home — or in finding them a new one.

docs.lead_paragraph: For nearly a century, linguists have been struggling to unseat the accumulated dogma that “masquerades as common sense,” as the American linguist Leonard Bloomfield put it in 1933. That’s the challenge that faces every developing science, but linguistics seems to have had a harder time than most. People who readily accept the principles of modern economics, psychology and biology still cling to notions about language that are as antiquated as a belief in physi­ocracy or leeching.

docs.lead_paragraph: In late August 1945, with the work of the Office of Strategic Services, the United States’ wartime intelligence agency, winding down, Col. John Coughlin, commander of the O.S.S. detachment in Ceylon, called a field agent named Jane Foster to his bungalow. Foster assumed she was in trouble, since she usually was. (She liked to say she was the organization’s “most-threatened-with-court-­martial person.”) Instead Coughlin poured her a drink and asked if she would volunteer to report on the postwar transition in Java. Wouldn’t she! Foster, who spoke Malay and had lived in Batavia, had already told a friend about her “confidential plan” to infiltrate a small Indonesian island and emerge as “the Great White Queen of Bali.” The friend half-believed her. With Foster, she recalled, “you could never tell.”

docs.lead_paragraph: GOING HAWAIIAN: Sarah Vowell hits No. 5 on the hardcover nonfiction list with “Unfamiliar Fishes,” her wry account of the annexation and Americanization of Hawaii. What other writer would describe the first encounters between Hawaiians and missionaries as like “some sort of clunky prequel to ‘Footloose’ ”? Vowell also includes an exegesis of the cheesy 1987 surf flick “North Shore,” but insists she approaches wave-riding as a purely spectator sport. “I do love watching surfers,” she said in an e-mail. “I’m especially entranced by that moment they gather together offshore waiting for a wave. Maybe they’re out there talking trash, but from the sand it’s the perfect image of camaraderie. In the book I quote a hula scholar friend who calls surfing, like hula, quintessentially Hawaiian. The missionaries thought hula was ‘satanic.’ They were less offended by surfing. I read one missionary diatribe that predicted it would die out once the Hawaiians became accustomed to being fully clothed.”

docs.lead_paragraph: IN the bungling and bellicosity that constitute the back and forth of history, worsened by natural disasters and unprovoked cruelty,  humble citizens pay the highest price. To be a traveler in such circumstances can be inconvenient at best, fatal at worst. But if the traveler manages to breeze past such unpleasantness on tiny feet, he or she is able to return home to report: “I was there. I saw it all.” The traveler’s boast, sometimes couched as a complaint, is that of having been an eyewitness, and invariably this experience — shocking though it may seem at the time — is an enrichment, even a blessing, one of the life-altering trophies of the road.

docs.snippet: Two finalists were eliminated from “American Idol” on Thursday, Naima Adedapo and Thia Megia, as a results episode of the Fox reality show attracted an impressive 22 million viewers.
docs.lead_paragraph: Two finalists were eliminated from “American Idol” on Thursday, Naima Adedapo and Thia Megia, as a results episode of the Fox reality show attracted an impressive 22 million viewers, according to Nielsen’s estimates. The audience for “Idol” lifted Fox far ahead of its network rivals on the night and provided a boost to Fox’s hidden-camera special with Howie Mandel, “Mobbed,” which delivered a solid 10.8 million viewers at 9 p.m. following “Idol.” ABC’s “Grey’s Anatomy” (12.7 million) edged past CBS’s “CSI” (12.5 million) to lead that time slot, but CBS ranked second for the night over all, earning its best ratings at 10 with “The Mentalist” (13.9 million) and strong results at 8 and 8:30 for the sitcoms “The Big Bang Theory” (11.7 million) and “Rules of Engagement” (8.2 million). ABC was third as 6.3 million tuned in to “Wipeout” at 8 and 7.6 million at 10 for “Private Practice.” NBC placed a very distant fourth with mostly repeats of its comedy line-up. On Bravo on Wednesday, the eighth season finale of “Top Chef” delivered 2.8 million viewers, slightly more than the audience who watched the series’ prior season conclusion (2.7 million).

headline.main: ‘Idol’ Attracts 22 Million Viewers

docs.abstract: The Syrian port city of Latakia is particularly interesting because the town and province are the heartland of the Alawites, a Shiite sect that produced the ruling Assad family and much of the current governing elite.
docs.snippet: The Syrian port city of Latakia is particularly interesting because the town and province are the heartland of the Alawites, a Shiite sect that produced the ruling Assad family and much of the current governing elite.
docs.lead_paragraph: My cigarette days are well over but the name Latakia still brings up physical memories of “Turkish” tobacco. The Syrian port city was part of the Ottoman empire, is very near the Turkish border, and has a long connection with the tobacco trade. It’s in the news now for protests against the government of Bashar al-Assad. Latakia is particularly interesting because the town and province are the heartland of the Alawites, a Shiite sect that produced the ruling Assad family and much of the current governing elite. (In the wake of the Ottoman collapse in the early 20th century, there was an on-again-off-again Alawite “state” based in and around Latakia until 1944, when it integrated with Syria.)

headline.main: Holding Syria Together

docs.abstract: An exhibition of figural art, in a wide array of styles and media, presents the human form from a different perspective.
docs.snippet: An exhibition of figural art, in a wide array of styles and media, presents the human form from a different perspective.
docs.lead_paragraph: The human form is so pervasive in Western art that it is almost impossible to imagine our visual culture without it. The artists who gave us the Parthenon, the Mona Lisa and “Guernica” lived in vastly different worlds, yet they all channeled the essences of those worlds into their representations of the figure. There are no such epochal examples among the 43 works in “Human Connections: Figural Art From the Bruce Museum Collection.” But in this small, dense show, the Bruce asks us to think about the figure in art in a novel way. In most museum shows, we look at the subject — a painter or period or motif — through the lens of art history. Here, we are meant to see a range of artworks through the prism of the human body.

headline.main: Through the Prism of the Human Body

docs.abstract: In columns of statistics, Southern slaveholders read a terrifying prophecy.
docs.snippet: In columns of statistics, Southern slaveholders read a terrifying prophecy.
docs.lead_paragraph: A little knowledge is a dangerous thing; a lot of it can be deadly. Such was the case on the eve of the Civil War. Among all the events that touched off the great conflict — John Brown’s raid in 1859, Abraham Lincoln’s presidential victory in 1860 — there is one that has been strangely ignored by most historians. True, it was less dramatic than the others. It occurred when enumerators traveled from door to door throughout America, counting up Easterners and Westerners; Northerners and Southerners; blacks and whites; freemen and slaves. The numbers that they came up with helped to split apart the Union.

headline.main: The Census of Doom

docs.abstract: The International Court of Justice rejected a claim by the former Soviet republic of Georgia accusing Russia of ethnic cleansing in two rebel enclaves.
docs.snippet: The International Court of Justice rejected a claim by the former Soviet republic of Georgia accusing Russia of ethnic cleansing in two rebel enclaves.
docs.lead_paragraph: The International Court of Justice on Friday rejected a claim by the former Soviet republic of Georgia accusing Russia of ethnic cleansing in two rebel enclaves. The court, the judicial arm of the United Nations, ruled that it had no jurisdiction to decide the case, but made no decision on the merits of the accusation. In a statement on its Web site, the court said Georgia violated procedure by failing to hold direct talks with Russia over the dispute before going to court. Georgia filed the complaint in the midst of its war with Russia in August 2008, accusing Moscow of complicity in the forceful expulsion of ethnic Georgians from Abkhazia and South Ossetia. docs.lead_paragraph: Perhaps no aspect of baseball has received more statistical scrutiny over the last decade than pitchers’ control over the outcomes of balls in play. Ever since a paralegal named Voros McCracken posted a theory on the Internet in 1999 that pitchers could exert influence only on their strikeouts, walks and home runs allowed — leaving everything else up to fielders and luck — researchers have pored over a century’s worth of data on batting averages on balls in play. It turns out that McCracken and his detractors were partly right: although some pitchers are in fact more hittable than others, figuring out which ones they are while they are active is exceedingly hard.

headline.main: Keeping Score: Statistic Combines Physics and Luck

docs.abstract: The Easter bunny was No. 1 at the North American box office over the weekend as the animated and live-action hybrid “Hop” sold an estimated $38 million in tickets.
docs.snippet: The Easter bunny was No. 1 at the North American box office over the weekend as the animated and live-action hybrid “Hop” sold an estimated $38 million in tickets.
docs.lead_paragraph: The Easter bunny was No. 1 at the North American box office over the weekend as the animated and live-action hybrid “Hop” sold an estimated $38 million in tickets, performing far above expectations. The release from Universal Pictures cost $63 million to make, and audience-interest surveys indicated it would open to about $25 million in ticket sales. But a strong, whimsical marketing campaign did the trick, aided by the comedian Russell Brand, who gave voice to the main character, the Easter Bunny’s teenage son, right. Teenage girls, it turns out, find Mr. Brand as hilarious as many adults find him irritating. Summit Entertainment’s “Source Code,” an action thriller starring Jake Gyllenhaal, was second with about $15 million in ticket sales, according to Hollywood.com, which compiles box office data. “Insidious,” an extremely inexpensive horror film from FilmDistrict, was third with about $13.5 million in sales. “Insidious” cost only $1 million to make, according to Jason Blum, a producer of the film. “Diary of a Wimpy Kid: Rodrick Rules” (20th Century Fox) was fourth with about $10 million, lifting its two-week total to $38.4 million. “Limitless” (Relativity Media) was fifth, selling roughly $9.4 million in tickets for a three-week total of $55.6 million.

headline.main: ‘Hop’ Is Off to a Surprisingly Robust Start

docs.abstract: “Nine Circles,” a play by Bill Cain, is the winner of the 2011 Harold and Mimi Steinberg/American Theater Critics Association New Play Award.
docs.snippet: “Nine Circles,” a play by Bill Cain, is the winner of the 2011 Harold and Mimi Steinberg/American Theater Critics Association New Play Award.
docs.lead_paragraph: “Nine Circles,” a play by Bill Cain, is the winner of the 2011 Harold and Mimi Steinberg/American Theater Critics Association New Play Award. This year’s $25,000 prize, which honors a playwright for work that had its premiere outside New York City in the previous year, was presented to Mr. Cain on Saturday at the Actors Theater of Louisville during the Humana Festival of New American Plays. “Nine Circles” tells the story of a young American soldier accused of an atrocity in Iraq; it was originally produced at the Marin Theater Company in Mill Valley, Calif. This is the second straight year that Mr. Cain, who is also a producer and director, has won the award. Last year his play “Equivocation” took the honors following a run at the Oregon Shakespeare Festival. It then was staged at the Geffen Playhouse in Los Angeles and the Manhattan Theater Club at City Center. Two other playwrights were honored with citations and prizes of $7,500 each: Kathryn Grant for “The Good Counselor” and David Bar Katz for “The History of Invulnerability.”

docs.lead_paragraph: Parents of small children probably know James McMullan as the creator (along with his wife, Kate) of the popular picture book “I Stink!” about the nightly rounds of a profoundly disgusting but hard-working New York City garbage truck. He is also enshrined in disco lore for the paintings he did more than 30 years ago for New York magazine that became the visual inspiration for “Saturday Night Fever.” But these days Mr. McMullan is much better known for the elegantly expressive show posters he makes for Lincoln Center Theater. Last week a large selection of those posters — for plays and musicals like “Ah! Wilderness,” “Carousel,” above, and “South Pacific” — went on display near the theater they helped promote, at the New York Public Library for the Performing Arts at Lincoln Center. The posters and other work will remain on view at the library through June 11. On Monday Mr. McMullan will join a fellow theatrical graphic artist, Frank Verlizzo, known as Fraver, at the library for a discussion about poster making.

headline.main: ‘I Stink!’ Illustrator Shows Elegant Work

docs.abstract: Chico Trujillo, a local favorite, relies on cumbia, the beat heard in countless variations across Latin America.
docs.snippet: Chico Trujillo, a local favorite, relies on cumbia, the beat heard in countless variations across Latin America.
docs.lead_paragraph: SANTIAGO, Chile — Lollapalooza Chile has introduced me to a world-class party band: Chico Trujillo, a local favorite who had a huge crowd shouting along. Every party band needs a rhythm, and Aldo Asenjo, the band’s leader and singer, relies on cumbia, the beat heard in countless variations across Latin America. Cumbia often trots calmly, but Chico Trujillo’s version gallops, bounding along; now and then, the music switches into rumba, equally upbeat. Mr. Asenjo sings lyrics as chattery and percussive as some hip-hop, taking on the ups and downs of love and life, with his voice answered by chortling horns — did he borrow the arranging idea from ska bands? — and a tootling, circusy organ. Syncopation, momentum and a way of romping through pain — a party band needs them all, and Chico Trujillo has them.

headline.main: Lollapalooza Chile: A World-Class Party Band

docs.abstract: Bill James wants to know: “Why are we so good at developing athletes and so lousy at developing writers?”
docs.snippet: Bill James wants to know: “Why are we so good at developing athletes and so lousy at developing writers?”
docs.lead_paragraph: Bill James is rattling his sabremetrician-ness again. On Wednesday, he published an essay in Slate, “Verlander and Shakespeare.” It’s pretty great for reasons highlighted by its subtitle, “Why are we so good at developing athletes and so lousy at developing writers?” Throw a brush-back pitch like that and you’re sure to start a conversation. So much to argue with! The premise itself. Two gross assumptions underlying the premise. Then, another level down, the issue of what “developing” means. And “good.” And “lousy.” And “we” — who does that refer to, exactly? Just wait till you get to the actual arguments.

headline.main: Shakespeare in Left Field

docs.snippet: Newly discovered 1840s murals of inlets, willows, lighthouses and sailing ships are being extricated this week from a house in East Baldwin, Me., for transfer to the Rufus Porter Museum and Cultural Heritage Center in nearby Bridgton.
docs.lead_paragraph: Newly discovered 1840s murals of inlets, willows, lighthouses and sailing ships are being extricated this week from a house in East Baldwin, Me., for transfer to the Rufus Porter Museum and Cultural Heritage Center in nearby Bridgton. The owners have donated three roomfuls of the scenery, painted by the muralist Rufus Porter’s nephew Jonathan Poor, along with underlying layers of plaster and lath, fireplace mantels and an entire staircase. The museum is raising $60,000 for the dismantling work, by the salvager David Ottinger, and is renovating an 1830s house that will accommodate the acquisition. Poor died in his early 40s, soon after completing the work for a local physician, perhaps because mural painting was a hazardous profession. “My supposition is that all the materials they worked with were poisonous,” Julie Lindberg, the Porter museum’s curator, said.

headline.main: Maine Museum to Get Newly Discovered 1840s Murals

docs.abstract: Katie Couric sits down with the magazine.
docs.snippet: Katie Couric sits down with the magazine.
docs.lead_paragraph: Apparently, it’s official: Katie Couric will no longer anchor the “CBS Evening News.” It’s hardly a surprise. She has been hinting at a move for ages, and speculation that she wouldn’t last has been gurgling pretty much since her first day in the anchor’s chair five years ago. But rarely was she ever so open with her ambivalence about the job as she was in an interview with Andrew Goldman, which appears in the April 10 issue of the magazine but which we’re publishing online now. Goldman conducted it on Friday, March 25, the day before Couric took off for a pre-big-news vacation to Turks and Caicos. Although she wouldn’t confirm that she was leaving the show — she was more interested in discussing her new book, “The Best Advice I Ever Got: Lessons From Extraordinary Lives” — she expressed some regrets about trying to push the nightly-news genre too far too fast and she floated a theory (though she wouldn’t put her name behind it) that CBS’s local news lead-ins might have kept her mired in third place.

headline.main: When Katie Couric Met Andrew Goldman

docs.abstract: ‘The Pale King” is an incomplete, complex, confounding, brilliant novel. In other words, the perfect coda to an author’s troubled life.
docs.snippet: ‘The Pale King” is an incomplete, complex, confounding, brilliant novel. In other words, the perfect coda to an author’s troubled life.
docs.lead_paragraph: Every writer dies, probably, still intending to write something. It’s a basic fact of (to put it slightly trivially) scheduling: the time lines of mortality and ambition rarely coincide. Thomas Aquinas finished only the first two sections of his “Summa Theologica” — a work that would loom over philosophical thought for centuries — before (according to some biographers) he hit his head on a branch while riding a donkey and plunged into his final illness. Walter Benjamin worked for 13 years on his magisterial “Arcades Project” but left it unfinished when he committed suicide to avoid falling into the hands of the Nazis. The list could go on almost indefinitely, with works snuffed out by illness (Flaubert’s “Bouvard and Pécuchet”) and genocide (Némirovsky’s “Suite Francaise”) and alcoholic dissipation (Flann O’Brien’s “Slattery’s Sago Saga”). The loss is particularly hard when an author seems to have been really humming along — when the last big thing was a masterpiece and the next one promised to be another. “Dostoyevsky,” the novelist Norman Rush has said, “died still intending to write another volume of ‘The Brothers Karamazov.’ It’s like a knife in my heart that he didn’t.”

headline.main: David Foster Wallace’s Unfinished Novel — and Life

docs.snippet: A trained pastry chef, twice-published author and self-christened food creative hosts lunches in her  226-square-foot apartment in Paris’s Belleville neighborhood.
docs.lead_paragraph: “The only place I don’t cook in is my bathtub,” Rachel Khoo marvels. A trained pastry chef, twice-published author and self-christened food creative, Khoo hosts lunches at La Petite Cuisine à Paris, or the Little Paris Kitchen, in her 226-square-foot apartment in Paris’s Belleville neighborhood. The “little kitchen” concept might be a considerable hindrance to most chefs, but Khoo has made the most of it. “It’s like I’m on a constant camping holiday,” she says of the two gas rings and toaster oven at her disposal, and the resourcefulness that has sprung from them. She has whipped up Eton mess à la française, lemon and lavender roast chicken, tonka bean soufflé, and croque madame muffins. Khoo’s favorite dish so far, pot au feu fajitas (melt-in-your-mouth beef stew and fresh vegetables in a tortilla with sauce from the pot au feu), summarizes the spirit of her book: “It’s not quite French, but it takes on the initial French flavors.”

headline.main: Lean Cuisine | Paris’s Tiniest Kitchen

Gagarin. Two Russian cosmonauts and an American astronaut are scheduled to ride the Yuri Gagarin rocket into orbit, on their way to the International Space Station; the honorary naming was a departure from the usual Russian practice of numbering rockets. The rocket, scheduled to launch before Tuesday, also has a portrait of Mr. Gagarin painted on the side. He was only 27 years old when he made his first and only journey into space, and he later died in a jet airplane crash. The Soyuz model booster was being fueled Monday evening on the same launch pad where Mr. Gagarin blasted off on his flight on April 12, 1961, which began with his words “Let’s go.”

docs.abstract: ‘‘Cocktail Culture,” an exhibition opening soon at the Rhode Island School of Design, must have been inspired by ‘‘Mad Men.’’
docs.snippet: ‘‘Cocktail Culture,” an exhibition opening soon at the Rhode Island School of Design, must have been inspired by ‘‘Mad Men.’’
docs.lead_paragraph: The current fads for artisanal liquor, louche bars and everything ‘‘Mad Men’’ must have inspired ‘‘Cocktail Culture: Ritual and Invention in American Fashion, 1920-1980,’’ an exhibition that opens Friday (and continues through July) at the Museum of Art at the Rhode Island School of Design. It features more than 220 artifacts, including a Dansk ice bucket, a Norman Bel Geddes soda siphon, Paco Rabanne purses and lots of little black dresses (as well as the red one shown below, by Norman Norell). The show begins in the 1920s, when American cocktail culture was mostly confined to the home, and the French, with their beaded cocktail dresses and René Lalique Art Deco glass, set the standard for a night on the town. But the most durable pieces, the ones that you’d still want to break out for guests today, date from the 1950s, when every hour was happy hour and cocktail design was strained through a Modernist sieve. Consider Donald Colflesh’s 1959 silver-plated pitcher for Gorham (below), whose sleek form seems to respond only to one request, essential and elegant: martini, straight up.

headline.main: Highballs and High Art

docs.abstract: You don’t have to like the new Republican budget, but you do have to respect it.
docs.snippet: You don’t have to like the new Republican budget, but you do have to respect it.
docs.lead_paragraph: You do not have to like the long-term budget that Paul Ryan and the House Republicans have released this morning. There’s plenty in the plan for liberals to hate, moderates to doubt, and conservatives to question. But you do have to respect it. As my colleague David Brooks writes today, it is “the most comprehensive and most courageous budget reform proposal any of us have seen in our lifetimes.” It puts flesh on the bones of the standard-issue conservative pledge to limit government’s growth, and it does so not with evasive pledges on process (like the risible idea of a balanced budget amendment) or dishonest suggestions that the deficit can be erased by defunding N.P.R. and slashing foreign aid, but by attacking entitlement spending deeply and directly. George W. Bush touched the third rail of American politics with his Social Security gambit, and lived to regret it. With their proposal to transform Medicare from an open-ended entitlement to a system that provides support for seniors’ premiums, Ryan and the Republicans are reaching out and grabbing it with both hands. In the process, they are being brutally honest with the American people, in ways that the Obama White House has repeatedly refused to be, about the scale of the deficit challenge and the scope of the reforms needed to address it.

headline.main: Paul Ryan and the Triumph of Policy

docs.lead_paragraph: Molly Bloom’s wandering soliloquy in James Joyce’s “Ulysses” was the inspiration for “The Sensual World,” the title song from Kate Bush’s 1989 album, but at the time the Joyce estate would not give her approval to use the words in her lyrics. Now Ms. Bush has received the long-awaited permission to use the text, and she has rerecorded the song, which she renamed “Flower of the Mountain,” according to BBC News. Ms. Bush said she was “delighted” to have the chance “to fulfill the original concept.” The new track will be released in May on “Director’s Cut,” her first new album in six years.

headline.main: Kate Bush Has Permission to Use Words of James Joyce

docs.lead_paragraph: The shoegazer singer Tamaryn, who started a North American tour with the Raveonettes last week, has learned a thing or two about stage makeup. “I don’t always use primer on my eyes, and I never wear powder — I like everything to be a little dewy and sexual looking,” said the singer during a pretour shopping spree in SoHo. (Stops included M.A.C. and Sephora.) She recently discovered Super, Dr. Nicolas Perricone’s new collection, at its flagship in Berkeley, Calif. — the band is based in San Francisco — and swears by the First Blush Brightening Serum: “I’ve been using it over makeup to set it and have a bit of a glow.” Other must-haves include Osis Mattifying Powder (“I sprinkle it in my hair and it looks teased”), Stila Kajal Eye Pencil in black (“looks better the next day”), Frederic Malle Une Rose (“androgynous but romantic — plus the traditional Goth girl scent is rose water”) and Tom Ford Bruised Plum Lip Color (“it’s like neu-Goth, because it’s sheer”). But the singer is always looking to evolve with her look: “I really want to start wearing brown lipstick. I’ve been watching a lot of ‘My So-Called Life’ lately, and they all have that brown lipstick! I think the ’90s are what it’s all about right now.”

headline.main: Stage Beauty | Tamaryn

docs.lead_paragraph: Let’s say it is your friend’s birthday. Should you ask her what she wants and simply buy her that present, or should you thoughtfully think of something yourself and surprise her? An article in the Journal of Experimental Social Psychology suggests the first route is best. Francesca Gino and Francis Flynn conducted 5 separate studies and found that people were more pleased by gifts they explicitly requested. They were also quite pleased by gifts of cash. Givers believe that people like surprises but giftees just want what they want.

headline.main: Birthday Time

docs.lead_paragraph: A two-hour installment of “Dancing With the Stars” attracted an average of 21.4 million viewers on Monday, lifting ABC to first place in the night’s ratings ahead of CBS and its college basketball coverage, according to Nielsen’s estimates. Although final audience figures for CBS’s live broadcast of the N.C.A.A. men’s championship game were not immediately available on Tuesday, preliminary overnight estimates were down slightly compared with last year, when 23.9 million watched the title matchup on CBS. Despite that modest decline, the game’s ratings were still high enough that CBS might have led the night over all were it not for lower ratings preceding the basketball coverage for sitcom reruns at 8 and 8:30, “The Big Bang Theory” (9.6 million) and “Rules of Engagement” (7.4 million). The repeats lagged in comparison with ABC’s 10 p.m. audience for “Castle” (11.7 million) following “Dancing With the Stars.” NBC ranked third with “Harry’s Law” at 10 (7.4 million) following a rerun of “Chuck” at 8 (2.5 million) and “The Event” at 9 (3.9 million). Fox was fourth with repeats of “House” (4.4 million) and “The Chicago Code” (3.9 million).

headline.main: ‘Dancing’ Carries ABC Again in Ratings

docs.lead_paragraph: Handel liked the myth of Acis and Galatea so much that he set it to music twice, and did plenty of tinkering with both versions. As told in Ovid’s “Metamorphoses,” the story is simple and brief: the shepherd Acis and the sea nymph Galatea are happily in love, but the Cyclops Polyphemus loves Galatea too. docs.snippet: The documentary “Blank City” looks at iconoclastic downtown New York filmmakers in the late 1970s and early ’80s.
docs.lead_paragraph: Céline Danhier’s “Blank City” uses conventional documentary methods — talking-head reminiscences intercut with clips from the archives — to explore the work of a group of aggressively anticonventional artists. This is not a criticism. The movie is about the iconoclastic filmmakers clustered in the East Village and Lower East Side of Manhattan in the late 1970s and early ’80s. The chaotic, fast-moving, hazily remembered scene they created deserves and benefits from the scholarly consideration Ms. Danhier offers. A dogged journalist and a careful, enthusiastic cultural historian, she illuminates a hectic and fascinating place and time, bringing it back to life and tracing its continuing influence.

headline.main: That ’80s Moment When Nothing and (Almost) Everything Mattered

docs.abstract: The photographer Steven Sebring takes a painterly approach to portraiture in “Illuminations,” his current show of monumentally scaled images of American cultural icons who have left indelible mark on the Manhattan’s downtown culture.
docs.snippet: The photographer Steven Sebring takes a painterly approach to portraiture in “Illuminations,” his current show of monumentally scaled images of American cultural icons who have left indelible mark on the Manhattan’s downtown culture.
docs.lead_paragraph: Fine art and fashion make a pretty agreeable cocktail. For the photographer Steven Sebring, each is an ingredient in a body of work that spans several decades and a multitude of photographic techniques. Mr. Sebring takes a painterly approach to portraiture in his current show of monumentally scaled images of American cultural icons — poets as he calls them — who have left indelible mark on the Manhattan’s downtown culture. Viewed at close range, his subjects radiate light like stained glass — hence the title of the show, “Illuminations,” at Milk Studios in Chelsea. At a distance, the features of his subjects — writers and musicians including Jim Carroll, Joey Ramone, Richard Hell and Patti Smith — seem almost animated, swimming into focus as the viewer backs away.

headline.main: Steven Sebring’s Downtown Faces

docs.abstract: Salento Farm in Shelton, Conn., may not be monocultural, but it’s close to it.
docs.snippet: Salento Farm in Shelton, Conn., may not be monocultural, but it’s close to it.
docs.lead_paragraph: Locavores who criticize monocultural farming obviously do not have Patrick Salvati and Dorothy DeMarco in mind. Their Salento Farm in Shelton, Conn., may not be monocultural, but it’s close to it. They grow only garlic and eggplant. Their garlic is German hard neck, and they chop it up with garlic scapes, adding olive oil and Parmigiano-Reggiano to make a garlic pesto, so you can banish mint jelly forever for that spring lamb roast. They also dry and pulverize it to make first-rate pungent garlic powder to use in dry rubs, to season your pizza dough, and so forth. “Ours is all garlic, nothing else, not like the commercial brands,” Mr. Salvati said, as he won over a garlic powder skeptic at his new stand in the Greenmarket. Their tangy pickled eggplant is excellent on a bruschetta. In fall and winter, they sell the garlic heads, too.

headline.main: At This Farm, It’s All Garlic and Eggplant

docs.lead_paragraph: When Don Hill, who opened his eponymous downtown club in 1993 (and before that, the Cat Club and Kenny’s Castaways), died last Thursday, social media were buzzing with words of remembrance. Many people knew him as the man at the end of the bar, drinking tequila and Heineken, occasionally playing video games. “We did parties last month for the First Precinct and the Hells Angels,” said Paul Sevigny, who, along with Nur Khan, began working with Hill about seven months ago to bring some new blood to the place. “That’s how universally loved he was.” Loved, yes, but also a mystery even to those who knew him — details about his family and childhood remain fuzzy. “You’d go in there with someone who’d never been and you’d be like, ‘Oh, there’s Don!’ And people would be like, ‘There’s actually a Don Hill?’” said the makeup artist Mike Potter. “People didn’t know he was a real person.” Like many, Potter, a club regular in the ’90s, has Don Hill’s to thank for his career: After John Cameron Mitchell recognized him from the SqueezeBox party, the two became friendly, which led to Potter doing the makeup for “Hedwig and the Angry Inch.” Brendan Manning, of the New York City chapter of the Hells Angels, points out that Hill, whose memorial service is tonight at St. Patrick’s Cathedral in NoLIta, had booked — for $200 a week — “a guy named Bruce Springsteen,” back in the Kenny’s Castaways days. The Moment asked a few who knew Hill personally to tell us about him (in more than 140 characters).

headline.main: Remembering Don Hill

The publisher Little, Brown said on Wednesday that it had acquired a book that Mr. Abrams, the director of “Star Trek” and a creator of the television series “Lost,” “Alias” and “Felicity,” had conceived and will be written by Doug Dorst, the author of the supernatural crime novel “Alive in Necropolis.” A release from the publisher happily cited Mr. Abrams’s film and television credits and mentioned that Mr. Dorst is a graduate of the Iowa Writers’ Workshop and a three-time “Jeopardy!” champion. And Mr. Abrams said in a statement that “Doug is a genius,” adding that he “could not be more excited to collaborate with him on this completely original project.” Just what that project is neither Mr. Abrams nor Little, Brown is indicating, except to say that it is planned for a fall 2012 release on the Mulholland Books imprint. Watch for further clues as soon as we know where to find them.

docs.abstract: It appears that those who have to guard against more infectious diseases have lower average IQs than those who don’t.
docs.snippet: It appears that those who have to guard against more infectious diseases have lower average IQs than those who don’t.
docs.lead_paragraph: Some researchers subscribe to what is known as the parasite stress hypothesis. This holds that over the course of evolution the body faced a trade-off between maximizing intelligence and maximizing the power of the immune system. To test this Christopher Eppig, Corey Fincher and Randy Thornhill compared the IQ levels and disease stress in various American states. Sure enough, states where people have to guard against more infectious diseases (presumably because of climate) had lower average IQs. This is one of those studies where it is important to remember that correlation is not causation. Still, the researchers did find that after controlling for education and wealth, disease stress was the best predictor of state IQ.

headline.main: Bugs and Brains

docs.abstract: Why Republicans will nominate a dweeb to run against Obama in 2012.
docs.snippet: Why Republicans will nominate a dweeb to run against Obama in 2012.
docs.lead_paragraph: The Republican Party’s presidential-nominating process has always been run by elites. Oh, the voters have their brief moments of triumph, hoisting up an unelectable right-winger (i.e., Pat Buchanan) or an uncontrollable moderate (John McCain, the circa-2000 version). But the establishment always wins. Meeting in their K Street offices and communicating through organs like George Will’s column and National Review, the main financers and organizers settle upon a useful frontman, a reliable vessel for the party’s agenda who — and this is the crucial part — is blessed with the requisite political talent. Democrats have been known to mess that last part up and nominate a dweeb, but Republicans have generally understood that an agenda tilted toward the desires of the powerful requires a skilled frontman who can pitch Middle America. Favorite character types include jocks, movie stars, folksy Texans and war heroes.

headline.main: The G.O.P.’s Dukakis Problem

docs.abstract: The choreographer Stephen Petronio’s “Underland” at the Joyce Theater is a high-level entertainment, whose most seductive element — its score of songs by Nick Cave — is also its biggest handicap.
docs.snippet: The choreographer Stephen Petronio’s “Underland” at the Joyce Theater is a high-level entertainment, whose most seductive element — its score of songs by Nick Cave — is also its biggest handicap.
docs.lead_paragraph: There’s a visceral thrill to Stephen Petronio’s choreography that is unlike anything offered by other contemporary choreographers.  Legs whip round bodies with razor-edged ferocity; high, flying jumps erupt into the air; pelvises and torsos ripple through abrupt, unpredictable changes of direction, shifting from vertical to horizontal and back in the blink of an eye. The movement, with its improbable juxtapositions, seems to pour across the stage in an unquenchable flow, and yet it’s rarely too much for the eye to absorb.

headline.main: It’s Nick Cave’s World; They Just Dance in It

He was reborn months later, after he awoke from a nine-day coma, his memory wiped nearly clean of the details of his life — his early marriage, girlfriends, family, Navy service, thundering alcoholism, homelessness, jail time — and he had to relearn how to eat, walk and think at age 38. docs.abstract: After a two-month pause, immigration authorities will resume the deportations of Haitians who have been convicted of crimes in the United States.
docs.snippet: After a two-month pause, immigration authorities will resume the deportations of Haitians who have been convicted of crimes in the United States.
docs.lead_paragraph: After a two-month pause, immigration authorities will resume the deportations of Haitians who have been convicted of crimes in the United States. Immigration and Customs Enforcement began deporting Haitians in January, removing 27 that month, but stopped after one deportee died of choleralike symptoms shortly after arriving in Haiti and others fell ill. In new guidelines issued last Friday, the agency said it would limit deportations mainly to Haitians convicted of violent crimes and repeat offenders, who had also been ordered removed by an immigration court. Agency officials said they would not place a priority on deporting Haitian criminals who require medical treatment in this country. Catholic advocates said many of the first deportees had served their sentences and had been living without incident for years. The agency suspended the deportations after a Jan. 12, 2010, earthquake in Haiti.

headline.main: Haitian Deportations to Resume

docs.abstract: Sofia Sizzi’s love for lavish Italian fabrics was one of the reasons she started her women’s wear line, Giulietta.
docs.snippet: Sofia Sizzi’s love for lavish Italian fabrics was one of the reasons she started her women’s wear line, Giulietta.
docs.lead_paragraph: Giulietta, which had its debut in a whitewashed loft during New York Fashion Week, is helmed by Sofia Sizzi (above, center), a Florentine-born Manhattanite who is driven by a love for lavish Italian fabrics. “Is that really double-knit?” one observer whispered of a black wool suit consisting of skinny flared trousers, a hip-length narrow-lapeled jacket and a long fitted vest that could serve as a minidress to nouveau Twiggys. The 24-look collection includes a black wool sateen dress accented with a Peter Pan collar, a handmade lace widow skirt and a saffron printed pantsuit based on Sizzi’s sketch of a Baroque cathedral ceiling. The shoes — velvet, satin and felt wedges and heels (all vegan, to match the 33-year-old’s lifestyle) in salmon, saffron and cardinal red — attest to what Sizzi learned while working as an accessories designer at Gucci, Calvin Klein and Donna Karan. Clever ’60s proportions and mod collaborations with the milliner Patricia Underwood and the jeweler Thomas Bliven add a bit of nonecclesiastical zing. From $435 at Barneys New York.

headline.main: Ciao, Bella

docs.lead_paragraph: There’s been a shift in how we think about human evolution. Years ago, people tended to see evolution as a competition for survival of the fittest. But now there is more emphasis on the gentler virtues. People survive because they are really good cooperators. Research into hunter-gatherer cultures has contributed to this new understanding. People once believed that early humans lived in small kinship circles and fought to pass along their common genes.

docs.lead_paragraph: The director Kelly Reichardt is one of very few women in American independent cinema who has managed to have a sustained career making full-length features. Her small-scale, slow-burn tales of the lost and dispossessed, like “Old Joy” and “Wendy and Lucy,” have garnered critical acclaim for their larger social and political relevance. In her latest film, “Meek’s Cutoff,” opening Friday in New York, the lost are a group of pioneers crossing the Cascade Mountains in 1845, who find themselves wandering the high plain desert after they decide to take a shortcut. Here, Reichardt discusses her unorthodox take on the Western genre, starring her frequent collaborator Michelle Williams.

headline.main: O Pioneers! | Kelly Reichardt’s Anti-Western

docs.snippet: A remake of the 1981 comedy “Arthur” stars Russell Brand in the Dudley Moore role of the boozy billionaire.
docs.lead_paragraph: It would be conventional to describe “Arthur” as a vehicle for the talents of Russell Brand, who plays the boozy billionaire of the title, but that would be to get it backward. Mr. Brand, with his stringy hair, stretched-out body and nutty British demeanor, is more like the beast of burden, charged with hauling this grim load of mediocrity to the box office. The film, directed by Jason Winer and based on a fondly recalled 1981 comedy of the same name starring Dudley Moore, has been made according to a lazy and cynical commercial blueprint. You’ve seen it in the lesser work of Will Ferrell, Adam Sandler and most other male comedians who walk the line between popularity and overexposure. The star does his patented shtick, supported by a handful of blue-chip supporting performers, as the story lurches through contrived, seminaughty comic set pieces toward a sentimental ending.

docs.lead_paragraph: WHAT would you do with $600 billion in cash? If you’re the capital of the United Arab Emirates, rich in oil, the answer is easy: go shopping. Once aloof from the spendthrift ways of neighboring Dubai, Abu Dhabi — which, so far, has not experienced the unrest many Arab countries are facing — is now ticking off items on a five-star shopping list. Top-notch museums? New branches of the Louvre and Guggenheim are rising from the sands. High-profile events? The Abu Dhabi Grand Prix, Abu Dhabi Film Festival and Gourmet Abu Dhabi have made their debuts in recent years. Toss in a multibillion-dollar hotel project and a stunning new mosque and you have one of the world’s most ambitious new destinations.

docs.lead_paragraph: A close friend is getting married. When he invited us, I was pregnant and said, “I hope we can come, but it depends how new parenthood is treating us.” Since then, we’ve accepted and booked nonrefundable plane tickets. Now it occurs to me that our baby might not be welcome at the wedding. But I’m afraid to ask, because if we can’t bring him, we’ll have to miss it and eat the cost of the tickets. My plan is to feign ignorance, bring the baby and hope for the best. Is that wrong? Melanie, Boston

docs.abstract: Michelle Williams portrays a member of a pioneer family crossing Oregon Territory in “Meek’s Cutoff,” directed by Kelly Reichardt.
docs.snippet: Michelle Williams portrays a member of a pioneer family crossing Oregon Territory in “Meek’s Cutoff,” directed by Kelly Reichardt.
docs.lead_paragraph: The first thing you see in “Meek’s Cutoff,” after a hand-scrawled title card placing the action in the Oregon Territory in 1845, is a small group of settlers fording a river. It’s a treacherous, tedious undertaking, and Kelly Reichardt, the director of this tough, quiet revelation of a movie, films it in an uninflected style that makes everything feel at once mundane and mysterious. We are seeing the world more or less exactly as it looked to those hardy, foolish souls on screen (and almost forgetting to notice that most of them are actors we recognize from elsewhere). The way that world looked to them was unimaginably strange, every hill and rock loaded with portent, promise and menace.

docs.lead_paragraph: It may be that “Your Highness,” a self-conscious, sometimes overly self-satisfied goof about ye olde high times, may be better enjoyed in an herb-enhanced condition. Getting stoned is, after all, a running joke in this comedy, which is as thin as rolling paper and just as ephemeral. Certainly its milieu — a fantasy past filled with mythical beasts, a dwarf kingdom and bare-breasted wild women smeared in white who look as if they stepped off the cover of a classic punk album by the Slits — seems to have been hatched in an altered state. Conjoined laughing and groaning is often the point when jokes are calibrated to go up (or down) with smoke.

docs.lead_paragraph: In the first scene of Francisco Goldman’s passionate and moving autobiographical novel (or fictionalized memoir, depending on your bias), he travels to Paris with his young girlfriend, Aura Estrada. At her insistence, they go to the Jardin des Plantes to see the exotic salamanders Julio Cortázar wrote about in his famous story “Axolotl.” She wants to stare at them through the glass of their aquarium like the story’s protagonist. The wish to stare through glass to come to an understanding (of the axolotl, of the workings of a writer’s mind, of what cannot truly be understood) elegantly conveys the project of “Say Her Name,” this beautifully written account of Goldman’s short marriage to Estrada, a fiction writer who died in a bodysurfing accident in 2007, two years into their marriage, when she was 30.

docs.lead_paragraph: Bacteria containing an antibiotic-resistant “superbug” gene have been found in 2 of 51 tap water samples in New Delhi and in dozens of puddles and pools that children could play in, according to a report published Thursday in the journal Lancet Infectious Diseases. A team from Cardiff University in Britain found the gene, NDM-1, in 11 different types of bacteria, including those that cause cholera and dysentery. Bacteria with NDM-1 have caused fatal infections in people hospitalized in India, Pakistan and Bangladesh and in a few foreigners who visited those countries for surgery, but this is the first time they have been found in the environment. Their presence in water has not caused any known outbreaks of untreatable disease, but experts fear it could, especially in the rainy season.

headline.main: India: ‘Superbug’ Gene Found in Environment

docs.abstract: The Alabama Department of Public Health said that a contaminated intravenous nutritional supplement that was given to nine patients who died was due to a bacterial contamination in a water faucet.
docs.snippet: The Alabama Department of Public Health said that a contaminated intravenous nutritional supplement that was given to nine patients who died was due to a bacterial contamination in a water faucet.
docs.lead_paragraph: The Alabama Department of Public Health said Thursday that a contaminated intravenous nutritional supplement that was given to nine patients who died in hospitals last month was due to a bacterial contamination in a water faucet in the pharmacy where the supplement was produced. Dr. Donald E. Williamson, Alabama’s state health officer, said at a news conference on Thursday that the bacteria, Serratia marcescens, had been found in a faucet at Meds IV Pharmacy in Birmingham, a compounding pharmacy that makes medications that do not come premixed. From the faucet, the bacteria was introduced to tap water used to clean a container in which the nutritional supplement, called Total Parenteral Nutrition, was mixed. The bacteria has been found in the container, a stirring instrument and the amino acid powder used to make the supplement.

headline.main: Alabama: Bacteria Found in Pharmacy Faucet

docs.lead_paragraph: Apparently, banks in the United States don’t think their boardrooms were the problem. docs.lead_paragraph: AVNER DORMAN’S music works its magic by melding far-flung influences and making them sound natural together. Depending on the score, an inviting neo-Romantic fabric may bear touches of modernist acerbity; vigorous, complex rhythms; themes built on Middle Eastern and Indian modes; Baroque figuration; or the accents of pop and jazz. Extramusical notions often animate the music as well. “Mirage,” a string quartet, evokes both the desolation and the power of the Israeli desert; “Spices, Perfumes, Toxins!,” a kaleidoscopic percussion concerto, builds on the mingled allure and peril of the substances in its title.

docs.snippet: Bill Callahan, 44, sinks into his baritone on his latest album, “Apocalypse,” though he still mostly avoids face-to-face interviews.
docs.lead_paragraph: BILL CALLAHAN’S “Apocalypse” is a record that knows itself. Mr. Callahan, 44, one of our best lyricists and now — finally — a singer approaching excellence, uses his voice carefully, in a no-vibrato baritone, going down to Merle Haggard’s range. His recent songs have the pace of a more confiding time in music, when singer-songwriters in Nashville and Los Angeles were first working out what male sensitivity sounds like. “Apocalypse” can resemble an early-1970s record by Gordon Lightfoot or Mickey Newbury, but more heavy-hearted, slowed down by a quarter, with far fewer chords, and with words that embody rather than explain.

docs.lead_paragraph: To write about the trial of Adolf Eichmann is to put its most notorious court reporter, Hannah Arendt, in the dock. In the nearly 50 years since its publication, her account of those proceedings, “Eichmann in Jerusalem,” has come to overshadow its subject. The book, it is true, commands attention. It is a breathtaking admixture of genres (history, philosophy, journalism) and contains strong, often unconventional, moral judgments (especially her contempt for the Jewish leaders who cooperated with their murderers). It aims to render grand historical conclusions but remains unintentionally and inescapably personal.

docs.lead_paragraph: In his novel “The Notebooks of Malte Laurids Brigge,” Rilke writes of those who have been thrown away (die Fortgeworfenen), or what Michael Hulse translates as “the untouchables”: those sad “husks of men, spat out by fate,” as Rilke describes them, unworthy of being touched by either divine providence or simple human benevolence. Brigge has something of Dostoyevsky’s Underground Man seething within him, and also recalls the sordid unnamed narrator of Henri Barbusse’s novel “Hell”: misfits and spiritual lepers, indeed spat out by fate, these characters are simultaneously too outraged and too sensitive for civilization. They are precursors to perhaps the most notable misfit in 20th-century European fiction, Meursault from Albert Camus’s novella “The Stranger.”

docs.lead_paragraph: Many of us have probably on at least one cubicle-gray afternoon dreamed of lighting out in a rented U-Haul for some territory or other. Few who’ve acted on the impulse have made as excellent use of a sabbatical as Philip Connors has, and there are few territories left as wild and grand and as richly meaningful, or as spectacularly combustible, as the one Connors found almost a decade ago — New Mexico’s Gila Wilderness, the first designated wilderness in the history of the world, which also happens to be, as Connors puts it in his finely, wryly, at times poetically wrought first book, “the epicenter of American wildfire.”

docs.snippet: There are three productions of “Macbeth” under way in New York this month, but admirers of Shakespeare’s lighter work have an alternative: The Acting Company’s production of “The Comedy of Errors.”
docs.lead_paragraph: There are three very different productions of “Macbeth” under way in New York this month, but admirers of Shakespeare’s lighter work have an alternative: The Acting Company’s production of “The Comedy of Errors,” which begins performances at Pace University on Saturday night after a five-month national tour. Directed by Ian Belknap, this “Comedy of Errors” draws on Charlie Chaplin’s style of visually spare comedy routines as inspiration for staging the plot of two sets of identical twins accidentally separated at birth. The play, produced in association with the Guthrie Theater, is scheduled to run through April 17. It is part of the inaugural season of “Shakespeare at Pace,” a new endeavor that most recently included F. Murray Abraham’s Shylock in “The Merchant of Venice.”

headline.main: Pace Offers Shakespeare Fans an Alternative

docs.lead_paragraph: FOR two scorching days in Paris last May, the Champs-Élysées was closed to traffic, covered over with grass. Visitors traipsed through a forest of Lebanese cedar trees and snapped photos of goat pens and stacked pyramids of vegetables, with the Arc de Triomphe looming above. It was all part of Nature Capitale, a large-scale installation created by the French street artist Gad Weil, who timed it to coincide with International Biodiversity Day, an annual event sponsored by the United Nations. The spectacle drew two million visitors, among them two surprise guests: the French president, Nicolas Sarkozy, and his wife, Carla Bruni, who wore jeans and an untucked oxford shirt with rolled-up sleeves, providing a bit of barnyard chic in the Eighth Arrondissement.

docs.snippet: Luxury hotels and a high-speed train come to this hillside city in China.
docs.lead_paragraph: ON a misty afternoon in February, Lingyin Temple, a fourth-century Buddhist site that is one of China’s most important sanctuaries, felt more like a carnival than a place of worship. In large multigenerational packs, festive families were gathered for the Lunar New Year holiday, tossing fistfuls of ceremonial paper money into huge open fire pits and waving incense sticks as they jostled through crowds on their way to visit the 80-foot-high Buddha that is the building’s centerpiece. All the while they were downing fried tofu on sticks and corn on the cob and taking photos of everything on digital cameras. My family and I, possessing the only Western faces in the crowd, qualified as a photo coup — especially my towheaded toddler. “Look over here, foreign baby!” a young mother shouted as she held up her baby next to mine. The holiday period may officially last only a week, but the celebratory mood in Hangzhou seems to have permanently taken over this ever more vital city.

headline.main: The Poetry of Hangzhou

docs.abstract: In Mary Gordon’s emotionally engaging, smoothly flowing novel, former lovers, both now nearing 60, are reunited in Rome.
docs.snippet: In Mary Gordon’s emotionally engaging, smoothly flowing novel, former lovers, both now nearing 60, are reunited in Rome.
docs.lead_paragraph: Picture a woman of a certain age, alone in an Italian city, sitting in a cafe, pulling a spare chair against her table and nudging her coffee cup far from her water glass, so onlookers might imagine her to be accompanied. How sad, how brave, how hard to watch! In the film “Summertime,” Katharine Hepburn played such a woman, on a solo vacation in Venice, winking back tears while maintaining perfect posture and a rigid smile. But what if the lonely tourist weren’t as lonely as she appeared? What if a man was coming to lay claim to that chair, that coffee, that woman; and what if that woman wished he wouldn’t, “doesn’t at all want a coffee” and is “aware now that we’re at an age when we must take care not to be embarrassing.” Might the man’s presence make the woman lonelier than his absence? In her new novel, “The Love of My Youth,” so nostalgic in its title, Mary Gordon overturns sentimental assumptions, redirecting the reader’s sympathies from what could have been to what in fact was — and to what therefore followed. Using the passage of time as a soft pedal, she gentles the impact of a devastating affair, creating the record of a passion more safely reread than relived.

headline.main: Old Flames, Eternal City
headline.print_headline: The One Who Got Away

docs.abstract: Most of the great evolutionary innovations of life on earth are due to cooperation, a Harvard scientist argues.
docs.snippet: Most of the great evolutionary innovations of life on earth are due to cooperation, a Harvard scientist argues.
docs.lead_paragraph: What do colon cancer, ant colonies, language and global warming have in common? This might sound like the front end of a joke, but in fact it’s a serious challenge to the standard view of evolution. Martin A. Nowak, the director of the Program for Evolutionary Dynamics at Harvard, has devoted a brilliant career to showing that Darwin, and particularly his followers, batted only two for three. Random mutation and natural selection have indeed been powerful motors for change in the natural world — the struggle for existence pitting the fit against the fitter in a hullabaloo of rivalry. But most of the great innovations of life on earth, Nowak argues, from genes to cells to societies, have been due to a third motor, and “master architect,” of evolution: cooperation.

headline.main: How Evolution Explains Altruism
headline.print_headline: A Little Help From Your Friends

docs.abstract: The Museum of Modern Art presents a retrospective of the Soviet director Dziga Vertov (1896-1954), who celebrated the higher perception of cinema.
docs.snippet: The Museum of Modern Art presents a retrospective of the Soviet director Dziga Vertov (1896-1954), who celebrated the higher perception of cinema.
docs.lead_paragraph: IN many ways the Soviet filmmaker Dziga Vertov (1896-1954) was an artist of his time. A kindred spirit of the Constructivist artists who thrived in the wake of the 1917 October Revolution only to be stifled by the Stalinist policies of the 1930s, Vertov was a futurist at heart, a poet of the machine age. For a filmmaker in the reborn Russia the thrill of the new was palpable. Vertov, who saw theory and practice as inseparable, sought to uncover what made the young medium of moving images distinct from the other arts. Every film and every manifesto was an opportunity to examine the latent possibilities and harness the untapped power of cinema.

headline.main: Machine Age Poet, Born in Revolution, Stifled Under Stalin

docs.abstract: The new album by the Brooklyn group TV on the Radio is its first recorded outside New York.
docs.snippet: The new album by the Brooklyn group TV on the Radio is its first recorded outside New York.
docs.lead_paragraph: TV ON THE RADIO has made no secret of its catholic taste. Since 2001 this Brooklyn band — Tunde Adebimpe, Dave Sitek, Kyp Malone, Jaleel Bunton and Gerard Smith — has made ambitious rock with shades of post-punk, electronica and psychedelic jazz, and lyrics about global politics, love and language. The group made its latest album, “Nine Types of Light” (out Tuesday on Interscope), in Los Angeles, where Mr. Sitek now lives, its first recording outside New York; on Wednesday, the band will make its debut as headliner at Radio City Music Hall. But its members have not given up the indie ethos of the Brooklyn community that nurtured them. The band has already made videos for each song on the album, to be released both individually and edited into a film. “We as a band always have so many ideas for things that aren’t just musical,” Mr. Adebimpe said. “And for less than the price of a Maroon 5 video you can make a full-length feature.”

headline.main: Los Angeles, Perhaps, but Brooklyn Is Forever
headline.print_headline: Los Angeles, Perhaps, but Brooklyn Is Forever

docs.lead_paragraph: BEFORE he published “A Game of Thrones,” the first in his series of best-selling novels set on the mythical continent of Westeros, George R. R. docs.snippet: The Israeli pianist Omer Klein works in a modern-jazz mode, brisk and borderless.
docs.lead_paragraph: The Israeli pianist Omer Klein works in a modern-jazz mode, brisk and borderless, and yet his music vibrates with cultural specificity, projecting a sense of place. He’s among the current bumper crop of adaptable transplants from Israel to New York, like the saxophonist Eli Degibri, the multireedist Anat Cohen and her brother Avishai Cohen, a trumpeter. Unlike some of these peers Mr. Klein uses Middle Eastern folk elements as a patently important part of his platform, maybe the most important part.

headline.main: A Little Kick From the Middle East: Folk Spices the Jazz

docs.lead_paragraph: When encountering a first novel as self-assured, elegant, and perceptive as “The Free World,” David Bezmozgis’s intimate portrait of the Krasnanskys, a Jewish family from Latvia immigrating to the West in 1978, there’s a temptation to say that the author displays a maturity far beyond his years. But Mr. Bezmozgis, who is yet another vaunted member of The New Yorker’s “20 Under 40” group, was born in Riga, Latvia, in 1973, which makes him nearly the same age that Philip Roth and Leonard Michaels were when they respectively published “Portnoy’s Complaint” and “Going Places” in 1969. So it might be more accurate to say that Mr. Bezmozgis writes like someone exactly his age but from a previous generation.

docs.lead_paragraph: “Hop” was No. 1 at North American theaters for a second weekend in a row, selling an estimated $21.7 million in tickets for Universal Pictures (for a total of $68.2 million). But it was one of those weekends when a flop was the news: “Arthur,” a $40 million Warner Brothers remake starring Russell Brand, right, was a distant second with about $12.6 million — a terrible result considering the studio’s considerable marketing campaign. Brand burnout may have played a role. Mr. Brand, the comedian, known for his fingernails-on-a-chalkboard voice, has made recent appearances to promote his films — he is also a prominent member of the “Hop” cast (as the voice of E. B., left) — on outlets as varied as “American Idol” and the “Kids’ Choice Awards.” “Hanna,” a Focus Features release about a 16-year-old assassin, was a stronger-than-expected third with $12.3 million, according to Hollywood.com, which compiles ticket statistics. “Soul Surfer” (Sony Pictures Entertainment) was fourth with about $11 million; this drama, based on the true story of a girl who returns to surfing after losing her arm in a shark attack, received positive scores in exit polls. “Insidious” (FilmDistrict) was fifth with about $9.7 million for a two-week total of about $27 million. Also notable: “Your Highness,” a stoner comedy starring Natalie Portman and James Franco that cost Universal about $50 million, was a bomb, opening in sixth place with $9.5 million.

docs.snippet: Of the roughly 1,000 relics stolen from museums and archeological sites in Egypt since the sweeping protests began there in January, none were items of major importance, said Zahi Hawass, Egypt’s minister for antiquities, Agence France-Presse repo...
docs.lead_paragraph: Of the roughly 1,000 relics stolen from museums and archeological sites in Egypt since the sweeping protests began there in January, none were items of major importance, said Zahi Hawass, Egypt’s minister for antiquities, Agence France-Presse reported. “There is an inventory of everything, and it will be difficult for the items to leave the country,” Mr. Hawass told the Spanish newspaper El Mundo on Sunday, adding that the thieves were probably looters who lived near the sites, as opposed to organized criminals, and that they probably had little knowledge of the value of the goods they had pilfered. Many of the relics were taken from the Egyptian Museum in Cairo, which houses much of the King Tutankhamen collection, as well as the tombs of Hetep-ka at Saqqara and Em-pi at Giza.

headline.main: No Major Relics Stolen in Egypt

docs.abstract: James Richardson has received this year’s Jackson Poetry Prize, a $50,000 award presented to an American poet by Poets & Writers.
docs.snippet: James Richardson has received this year’s Jackson Poetry Prize, a $50,000 award presented to an American poet by Poets & Writers.
docs.lead_paragraph: James Richardson has received this year’s Jackson Poetry Prize, a $50,000 award presented to an American poet by Poets & Writers, a nonprofit organization for creative writers. Mr. Richardson’s latest collection, “By the Numbers: Poems and Aphorisms,” was released by Copper Canyon Press in November and was a finalist for the 2010 National Book Award. His previous collections include “Interglacial: New and Selected Poems and Aphorisms” (Ausable, 2004), a finalist for the National Book Critics Circle Award, and “Vectors: Aphorisms and Ten-Second Essays” (Ausable, 2001). The prize has been awarded since 2007 by a panel of three distinguished poets. This year’s panelists were Mark Doty, Rita Dove and Gerald Stern. Previous winners were Elizabeth Alexander, Tony Hoagland, Linda Gregg and Harryette Mullen.

docs.lead_paragraph: In June 2007, Julian Dibbell published an article in the Sunday Magazine about the shadow economy in virtual goods, focusing on “gold farmers” in China — workers hired by Chinese companies to play huge, multiplayer online games for the sole purpose of acquiring loot that could then be sold at a profit to regular players who didn’t have the time or the inclination to do it themselves and who use this purchased loot to increase their chances and status in these games. “For years now, the vast majority of virtual goods has been brought to retail not by players selling the product of their own gaming but by high-volume online specialty sites like the virtual-money superstores IGE, BroGame and Massive Online Gaming Sales — multimillion-dollar businesses offering one-stop, one-click shopping and instant delivery of in-game cash,” Dibbell wrote. “These are the Wal-Marts and Targets of this decidedly gray market, and the same economic logic that leads conventional megaretailers to China in search of cheap toys and textiles takes their virtual counterparts to China’s gold farms.”

headline.main: Virtual Gold, Real Money

docs.lead_paragraph: As a filmmaker, Bernardo Bertolucci has had a lasting impact on how audiences think of Asia and Africa, Buddhism and butter, but he has never won a Palme d’or – the top prize at the Cannes Film Festival. It is a gap on his trophy shelf that the organizers of the festival said they intended to correct at this year’s celebration. Mr. Bertolucci, whose films include “The Last Emperor,” “The Sheltering Sky,” “Little Buddha” and “Last Tango in Paris,” will be given an honorary Palme d’or at the opening ceremony of this year’s festival, it was announced on Monday. The festival has previously presented honorary awards to filmmakers including Woody Allen (in 2002) and Clint Eastwood (in 2009), and starting this year plans to make the distinction an annual tradition.

headline.main: Bertolucci to Receive Honorary Palme d’or at Cannes
