docs.abstract: Sporting contests sometimes turn on a math problem that referees must solve instantly with only their eyes and brains: projecting where a ball’s interrupted flight would have taken it.
docs.snippet: Sporting contests sometimes turn on a math problem that referees must solve instantly with only their eyes and brains: projecting where a ball’s interrupted flight would have taken it.
docs.lead_paragraph: Imagine that you and your best buddy are missile tracking engineers working for the Pentagon (nice steady job in these times!). The two of you played hoops for rival schools in your youth, and each of you believes he is better than the other. You challenge each other to a one-on-one grudge match in your backyard, the winner entitled to bragging rights forever. All your colleagues show up, some with video cameras to film the historic showdown. It’s an intense match, and both of you are giving it all you’ve got. The game goes right down to the wire. You are one point behind, and with just a few seconds to go, you uncork a buzzer beater. The ball travels in a graceful arc towards the basket. To your eyes, it seems certain to go in. At that very moment, a hefty twig descends from the tree above, strikes the ball and deflects it away. The buzzer sounds.

headline.main: Numberplay: Tracking the Ball

docs.snippet: CBS’s Sunday-afternoon coverage of the Masters golf tournament helped lift the network’s prime-time ratings.
docs.lead_paragraph: CBS’s Sunday-afternoon coverage of the Masters golf tournament helped lift the network’s prime-time ratings as well, as CBS topped the night for the fifth consecutive Sunday. Although final audience figures for the Masters were not available on Monday, preliminary overnight estimates were the second highest in 10 years, behind last year’s broadcast. Following the final round of that tournament, CBS’s “60 Minutes” delivered the largest audience in prime time, garnering 13.1 million viewers in the 7 p.m. hour. CBS’s reality shows “The Amazing Race” and “Undercover Boss” each drew 10.7 million viewers, at 8 and 9, while CBS’s “CSI: Miami” won the 10 p.m. hour with 10.2 million. ABC finished second, earning its best ratings at 8 for “Secret Millionaire” (9.1 million), while two hours of “Brothers & Sisters” averaged 6.5 million from 9 to 11 and lagged behind “The Celebrity Apprentice” on NBC (8.1 million). NBC was third with 4.3 million for “Dateline” at 7 and only 3.5 million for “America’s Next Great Restaurant” at 8. Fox was fourth with its animated comedies.

headline.main: Masters Helps CBS Master Prime Time

docs.lead_paragraph: In my column on Sunday April 10, I described the complex, fast-moving environment in which The Times’s foreign desk reports developments online and in print. A further challenge to journalists on the desk is deciding how to prioritize the news, especially given the volume and urgency of news in the current climate. While one might argue that in the digital medium there is unlimited space for news, in print the situation is different. The recent case of the retraction of a key assertion by Richard Goldstone, the South African jurist who led a panel investigating Israel’s invasion of Gaza two years ago, is a case in point.

headline.main: Tough Call on Goldstone Retraction

docs.lead_paragraph: A 22-year-old navy submarine crewman appeared in magistrate’s court in Southampton on Monday, charged with killing one of the vessel’s senior officers and wounding three crewmen in a burst of automatic rifle fire while the submarine was berthed in the city’s harbor last week. The suspect, Able Seaman Ryan Donovan, was not asked to enter a plea and will return to court on Wednesday. A police investigation has focused on the gunman’s motives, which British newspapers have reported as related to his having been denied use of a crew toilet and a request for shore leave. A navy inquiry is centering on how the seaman was cleared for high-security duty on the missile-carrying submarine despite postings on the Internet that revealed that he had legally changed his name to Reggie Moondogg before joining the navy and had written aggressive rap songs.

docs.abstract: If you’ve received a wedding invitation from an arty couple in the past few years, there’s a good chance it was printed by one of these New York letterpresses.
docs.snippet: If you’ve received a wedding invitation from an arty couple in the past few years, there’s a good chance it was printed by one of these New York letterpresses.
docs.lead_paragraph: From handmade hair accessories to artisanal pickles, there’s a metaphorical back-to-the-land movement for every profession. For graphic design, it’s letterpress, a labor-intensive printing process that creative types are taking up as an antidote to days spent staring at their iMacs. Produced on antique presses and characterized by heavily impressed lettering on thick paper, letterpress cards and stationery — if you’ve received a wedding invitation from an even vaguely arty couple in the past few years, chances are it was letterpress printed — are the graphic design equivalent of slow food. For designers who want to unplug, literally, letterpress is a chance to spend time refining their craft using a method that was considered old-fashioned long before the days of Photoshop. “People miss the hands-on experience of printing,” says Daniel Gardiner Morris, a fourth-generation letterpress printer and the founder of the Arm, the Williamsburg studio where many local printers have learned the basics of handling Industrial Revolution-era machinery. “Even if you don’t know anything about the process, when you pick up something that was printed on a letterpress, you know there’s something different about it. It was touched by human hands.” Here, the lowdown on five printers who are getting their fingers inky.

headline.main: Start the Presses

docs.lead_paragraph: This week A. O. Scott looks back at the trial and execution of St. Joan as recounted in the silent classic by the Danish filmmaker Carl Theodor Dreyer in “The Passion of Joan of Arc” (1928). The film is based on the transcripts from the trial and explores it from a political and religious perspective. “There’s something powerful and mysterious about beholding the image of a human face,” Mr. Scott says about the film’s use of close-ups to build a kind of spiritual intensity. The entire first half is a succession of close-ups, which, Mr. Scott says, “create a feeling of intimacy and confinement. And the drama, even the narrative itself, are contained within these faces.” The film is ultimately more concerned with emotion than politics, making it that much more of a human story. “‘The Passion of Joan of Arc’ creates an uncanny, unforgettable, almost unique sense of connection to its main character,” Mr. Scott says. “We may not ultimately understand Joan, but we know her.” Have you seen the film? Please share your thoughts.

headline.main: Critics’ Picks Video: ‘The Passion of Joan of Arc’

docs.abstract: A change in the Federal Bankruptcy Code failed to deal with whether competing plans are to be considered simultaneously or serially. There are also disclosure issues.
docs.snippet: A change in the Federal Bankruptcy Code failed to deal with whether competing plans are to be considered simultaneously or serially. There are also disclosure issues.
docs.lead_paragraph: Until October 2005, dueling Chapter 11 plans were a theoretical possibility, but a rare occurrence in reality. The Federal Bankruptcy Code contemplated that a debtor might lose its exclusive right to propose a plan, but bankruptcy courts routinely extended exclusivity and the debtor typically proposed the only plan in the case. The plan was often the result of negotiation and might look very different from the first plan proposed by the debtor, but there was only one plan.

headline.main: The Problem With Multiple Chapter 11 Plans

docs.lead_paragraph: The title figure in “A Screaming Man” never screams or shouts. He rarely raises his voice above the pleasantly conversational and sometimes hardly speaks at all, though his silences can be telling. He works as a pool man in a modest hotel in Chad, where, during the day, he watches over splashing children and lazily sunbathing adults and not much else. Come dusk, he gathers together the wet towels that have been discarded on the chaises and cordons off the pool. His employer calls him by his given name, Adam (played by Youssouf Djaoro, a tall and cool drink of water), but everyone else calls him Champ, a title reflecting a past glory that he wears as proudly as his dazzlingly white uniform.

docs.lead_paragraph: David Greenspan plays a demon sent spinning through time on a mission of salvation in “Go Back to Where You Are,” his endearingly daffy new play at the Peter Jay Sharp Theater at Playwrights Horizons. This particular demon was originally a failed actor from ancient Greece named Passalus, and on his sojourn in the 21st century he finds it useful to transform himself into a genteel British matron and former actress named Constance Simmons. All of this whimsy means that Mr. Greenspan the playwright has concocted a honey of a part for Mr. Greenspan the actor, one that allows him to deploy multiple voices and display multiple facets of his baroque, androgynous stage persona.

docs.lead_paragraph: In the week since Paul Ryan’s budget proposal hit Washington, there’s been significant liberal pushback against the idea that Ryan and the rest of the House Republican leadership deserve to be called “serious” or “brave.” If Ryan and Co. were actually courageous, the liberal argument goes, they would have proposed raising taxes, or demanded Medicare cuts for current seniors, or otherwise taken on more conservative shibboleths and right-leaning interest groups. Political bravery, in this view, requires more than just proposing a more rigorous version of your own faction’s usual proposals. It requires breaking out of the partisan box completely, and risking the ire of your own side’s ideologues as well as the wrath of your political opponents.

headline.main: Is Paul Ryan’s Budget Brave?

docs.lead_paragraph: LUCERNE, Switzerland — Lucerne is having a yearlong affair with Brahms. Through the various parts of the Lucerne Festival, Bernard Haitink has been conducting the Chamber Orchestra of Europe in a comprehensive Brahms cycle. During the piano festival in November, they presented the two piano concertos (with Emanuel Ax as soloist) and the two serenades. In the current Easter festival, they performed the second of three programs on Monday evening, and they offer the third on Wednesday. In the summer festival, in August, they will add two final concerts amid a smattering of Brahms performed by others (Claudio Abbado and the Lucerne Festival Orchestra, Christian Thielemann and the Dresden Staatskapelle).

headline.main: Lucerne, a Wagner City, Engages in Yearlong Affair With Brahms

docs.abstract: Are bullies amoral or are they simply cruel?
docs.snippet: Are bullies amoral or are they simply cruel?
docs.lead_paragraph: Are bullies amoral or are they simply cruel? That is to say, do they bully others because they don’t know the difference between right and wrong, or simply because they don’t care about other people’s feelings? Gianluca Gini, Tiziana Pozzoli and Marc Hauser studied this question for the Journal Personality and Individual Differences. They studied 719 children between the ages of 9 and 13 and found that those who engaged in bullying had advanced moral competence. They could make sophisticated distinctions between moral and immoral conduct. They scored low on measures of compassion, though. This reinforces a growing body of research that suggests knowing right from wrong is not necessarily connected to behaving rightly or wrongly. Moral lectures don’t work well, but telling people stories designed to arouse compassion might.

headline.main: Thoughtless or Careless

docs.abstract: Blacks have lower rates of drug use than whites during early adolescence, but this gap gets inverted as they age.
docs.snippet: Blacks have lower rates of drug use than whites during early adolescence, but this gap gets inverted as they age.
docs.lead_paragraph: Anastasia Vogt Yuan studied substance abuse among blacks and whites. In the journal Sociological Spectrum, she reports that blacks have lower rates of drug use than whites during early adolescence, but this gap gets inverted as they age. That is to say, whites are more likely to age out of drug use—they stop as they get older. Blacks, perhaps because of work, economic and family conditions, age out less, so by middle age they are using drugs more than whites. This would seem to put a dent in the theory that blacks suffer higher rates of drug use because they are more likely to grow up in single parent homes. If that were true, you’d see the effects in early adolescence. The evidence would seem to point to broader social influences.

headline.main: Substance Abuse in Black and White

After numerous Google searches (no luck), inquisitive e-mails (no luck) and one (lucky) Facebook search, we found the maker of the pin: 19-year-old Taj Melendez in Brooklyn, New York. “During art class in elementary school, we would do projects like these with perler beads,” says Melendez, who, like Space Invader, the street artist with a similar aesthetic, seems to shy away from attention rather than seek it out. He made his first pin, a replica of the men’s restroom icon, when he was 16. “I just wanted to start something, I wanted to stand out.” He sells his designs — bow ties, barrettes and an assortment of brooches like a thought bubble or a football — through his Web site ($55 to $75; go to bytaj.com). “I want to keep them special — that’s why I don’t create too many too fast.” When asked how Diaconu got her hands on that darling panda face, he shrugs with disbelief. “I have no idea,” he says. “But I sure was happy.”

docs.lead_paragraph: Broadway’s revival of “Anything Goes” won’t be going anywhere any time soon. On Wednesday, Roundabout Theater Company announced that its production of that Cole Porter musical, starring Sutton Foster as the evangelizing nightclub singer Reno Sweeney and Joel Grey as the milquetoast gangster Moonface Martin, will extend its run by about six months. The revival, directed and choreographed by Kathleen Marshall, is now planned to play at the Stephen Sondheim Theater through January 8; it was originally scheduled to close after July 31. (That’s roughly 184 more performances of cruise-ship based musical farce, so let’s hope everyone packed some additional swim trunks.) Reviewing this production of “Anything Goes” for The New York Times, Ben Brantley wrote that it “exudes the effervescence of a freshly poured gin fizz,” adding that when Ms. Foster “turns her toothy, triumphant smile on the audience there’s no doubt that she’s made many converts.”

headline.main: ‘Anything Goes’ Extends Into 2012

docs.lead_paragraph: Graffiti have been the elemental memes of political speech, from the walls of Pompeii to the New York subways to the Berlin Wall, in all the oppressed countries of this world. So it is all the more surprising that the epithet hurled by the Libyan “freedom fighters” to their former leader, and which graces the outer walls of the Benghazi Katiba in the photograph by Franco Pagetti that opens Robert F. Worth’s article, reads “el-Qaddafi walad al-Yahudiya,” or “Qaddafi, born Jewish.” In other words, Qaddafi the non-Muslim, the unclean. For a country that aspires to be democratic, old habits certainly die hard. It is a useful indication of the care to be taken in assuming that the so-called Arab Spring is a time of revolutionary social renewal.

headline.main: Libya’s Revolution

docs.lead_paragraph: Out of the nearly 1,000 plays vying to be developed by the Eugene O’Neill Theater Center in Waterford, Conn., eight have been chosen to undergo the expert development process during the center’s National Playwrights Conference in July. The winners, to be formally announced on Thursday, will take audiences from a movie set in Jordan, where a veteran relives the trauma of war, to a sleep-away camp in Maine, where the Nadelmans visit their hard-to-handle son. The plays, which will be performed at the conference, are: “The Nether,” by Jennifer Haley; “The Happiest Song Plays Last,” by Quiara Alegría Hudes; “Good Goods,” by Christina Anderson; “An Incident” by Anna Ziegler; “Acquainted With the Night,” by Keith Reddin; “Tell Us of the Night” by Keith Huff; “The Troublemaker Project” by Dan LeFranc; and “How We Got On,” Idris Goodwin. The O’Neill, which won the 2010 Tony Award for Regional Theater, has been a springboard for new works and artists to full productions on Broadway, Off Broadway and at major regional theaters.

docs.abstract: Adele continues her run on the pop charts this week, returning to the No. 1 spot.
docs.snippet: Adele continues her run on the pop charts this week, returning to the No. 1 spot.
docs.lead_paragraph: Adele continues her run on the pop charts this week, returning to the No. 1 spot and displacing Britney Spears in the process, and becoming the first artist this year to rack up album sales of 1 million. Her “21” (XL/Columbia) sold 88,000 copies in the United States, according to Nielsen SoundScan, climbing two spots to reach No. 1 on the Billboard album chart for the fourth time in its seven weeks of release. The album has sold a total of 1.03 million copies. (The album with the second biggest sales of the year so far is another rootsy, critically respected British import: Mumford & Sons’ “Sigh No More,” on the Glassnote label, which has sold 645,000 copies in the United States and lands this week at No. 8.) Ms. Spears’s “Femme Fatale” (Jive) falls to No. 2 in its second week, with 75,000 sales, a 73 percent drop from its opening week. Radiohead’s “King of Limbs” (Ticker Tape) climbed three spots to No. 3 in its second week of wide release, with 67,000 sales. The rap/rock band Hollywood Undead is close behind with 66,000 sales of its new album, “American Tragedy” (A&M/Octone). On Billboard’s Digital Songs chart, the top three songs from last week hold steady: Katy Perry’s “E. T.” remains No. 1 for a fifth week, selling 323,000 copies, while the Black Eyed Peas hold at No. 2 with “Just Can’t Get Enough” and Rihanna stays at No. 3 with “S&M.”

headline.main: Adele Back on Top

docs.snippet: As the disaster in Japan looms large, a writer remembers growing up in the tiny town that houses Indian Point.
docs.lead_paragraph: I GREW up in Buchanan, N.Y., a tiny, mostly working-class village in northern Westchester County, on the eastern shores of the Hudson, tucked into a crook where the river bends. My parents were public school teachers, and we lived in a split-level wood house near Lake Meahagh (pronounced MEE-haw), a manmade pond where my sister and I laced up our figure skates each winter and carved broad figure eights into its big, imperfect surface. Buchanan is a modest community (the village itself comprises less than two square miles); when people ask where I’m from, I usually say Peekskill or Croton, the two closest midsize towns. For the most part, Buchanan is known only to itself.

docs.abstract: Among the 19 features in contention for this year’s Palme d’or are Terrence Malick’s “Tree of Life,”  Pedro Almodóvar’s “La Piel Que Habito” (“The Skin I Live In”) and Lars Von Trier’s “Melancholia.”
docs.snippet: Among the 19 features in contention for this year’s Palme d’or are Terrence Malick’s “Tree of Life,”  Pedro Almodóvar’s “La Piel Que Habito” (“The Skin I Live In”) and Lars Von Trier’s “Melancholia.”
docs.lead_paragraph: We’re still not entirely sure what Terrence Malick‘s generational drama “The Tree of Life” will be, but we can safely say that it will be one of 19 new films contending for the Palme d’or at the Cannes Film Festival that were announced by the festival’s organizers on Thursday. Also on the feature competition slate for this year’s festival, which runs from May 11 to 22, are Pedro Almodóvar’s “La Piel Que Habito” (“The Skin I Live In”), starring Antonio Banderas as a plastic surgeon seeking his daughter’s rapists; “We Need to Talk About Kevin,” a drama directed by Lynne Ramsay (“Morvern Callar”) and starring Tilda Swinton and John C. Reilly; “Melancholia,” from the Danish filmmaker Lars Von Trier (“Antichrist”); “Sleeping Beauty,” from the novelist turned first-time filmmaker Julia Leigh; and “Ichimei” (“Hara-Kiri: Death of a Samurai”) from the Japanese director Takashi Miike. The festival’s opening night film, which is not shown in competition, is Woody Allen’s “Midnight in Paris.” Other features that will be shown out of competition this year include “Pirates of the Caribbean: On Stranger Tides,” directed by Rob Marshall, and, just to make things interesting, Jodie Foster’s latest film, “The Beaver,” starring Mel Gibson.

headline.main: Almodóvar, Von Trier and Malick in Cannes Competition Lineup

docs.snippet: “Carnage,” with a script by Roman Polanski and the “God of Carnage” playwright Yasmina Reza, will star Jodie Foster, Kate Winslet, Christoph Waltz and John C. Reilly as the Brooklyn parents brought together by their children’s playground fight.
docs.lead_paragraph: If you can’t easily locate a pair of squabbling, overeducated married couples to eavesdrop on, and don’t want to move to New York to do it, you can head to your local movie theater in a few months. “Carnage,” Roman Polanski‘s film adaptation of Yasmina Reza’s play “God of Carnage,” has been acquired for distribution by Sony Pictures Classics, which said on Thursday that it plans to release the film at the end of the year. The stage version of “God of Carnage,” which in 2009 won the Tony Award for best play, chronicles two Brooklyn couples who are brought together by a playground fight between their children, leading to a night of arguing, drinking and vomiting. Its original Broadway cast featured Marcia Gay Harden (a Tony winner), James Gandolfini, Hope Davis and Jeff Daniels (all Tony nominees). The film features a script written by Mr. Polanski and Ms. Reza, and will star Jodie Foster, Kate Winslet, Christoph Waltz and John C. Reilly.

headline.main: Sony Pictures Classics to Distribute Polanski’s ‘Carnage’

Empowerment, for the events have allowed officials here the confidence to tout their own democracy’s progress, however violent and fragile it still is. MeLellan’s film — sponsored by Sunspel, a historic English underwear manufacturer — centers on a storied boxing club in London’s East London and in particular on Ryan Pickard, the young, squinty-eyed knockout of a narrator. Pickard and his brother spar and sweat like sprinklers in the sun-drenched ring, wearing singlets, tees and fine cotton boxer shorts from the classic Sunspel line. With training time done, Ryan and his mates head to the local cafe to “get away from the missus,” show off their tattoos and debate who’s the greatest fighter of all time. A day in the life of a fighting lad.

docs.lead_paragraph: “The Mountaintop,” Katori Hall’s play about the Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., will make it to Broadway this fall, but with only one of the two high-profile actors who were expected to appear in it. Producers for the play said on Thursday that Samuel L. Jackson, the Academy Award-nominated star of “Pulp Fiction,” would portray Dr. King in the production, to be presented at the Bernard B. Jacobs Theater, with previews beginning Sept. 22 and an opening on Oct. 13; Kenny Leon, a Tony Award nominee for last year’s revival of “Fences,” will direct. Halle Berry, who was supposed to play Camae, a hotel maid at the Lorraine Motel in Memphis in Ms. Hall’s imagined account of the night before Dr. King’s assassination, will not be participating in the production as had been anticipated. In a statement, producers said, “Ms. Berry would not be appearing in the role due to child-custody issues.” “The Mountaintop,” which made its debut in London in 2009, won Ms. Hall the Olivier Award for best new play last year.

docs.abstract: Robert Whitman specializes in the art of the ephemeral, in this case two performances, occurring at once, miles apart, that inform each other.
docs.snippet: Robert Whitman specializes in the art of the ephemeral, in this case two performances, occurring at once, miles apart, that inform each other.
docs.lead_paragraph: IT might be simplistic or a little silly to say that Robert Whitman — the performance pioneer who is probably the least known member of the vanguard that gave birth to the American experimental theater scene in the 1960s — basically foretold the creation of the Internet in his work. But when you consider the evidence, it’s hard not to believe he created it himself. Decades before YouTube and years before the video camera became a common artist’s tool, Mr. Whitman, a kind of junkman of fleeting imagery, extolled the virtues of television “as a great way to collect stuff; besides what’s on the air, a camera on anything brings it in live.” In 1972, in “News,” the first of his telephone pieces, he enlisted people around the city to use pay phones to call in descriptions of what they were doing or seeing at that moment, which the radio station WBAI broadcast live, a kind of aural Twitter stream. In one of his earliest theater pieces, “American Moon,” in 1960, he split the audience apart in separate tunnels to give each person a slightly different sense of the action. In doing so, he fulfilled what the curator Lynne Cook once described as his distinctive desire to work “collectively to construct an experience intended for the solitary individual,” a phrase that could just as well describe a lot of the social and cultural architecture of the Web.

headline.main: Two Points of View, Miles Apart

docs.abstract: “The Conspirator,” Robert Redford’s latest turn as director, imagines the path of justice in the aftermath of Lincoln’s assassination.
docs.snippet: “The Conspirator,” Robert Redford’s latest turn as director, imagines the path of justice in the aftermath of Lincoln’s assassination.
docs.lead_paragraph: I happened to see “The Conspirator,” a new historical drama directed by Robert Redford, on the day that the Obama administration, reversing its earlier position, announced that Khalid Shaikh Mohammed and four others would be tried by a military tribunal for their suspected roles in the Sept. 11 attacks. This coincidence underscored the film’s topical relevance, which was hardly obscure to begin with. Its theme is the rule of law in the aftermath of a national tragedy, the assassination of Abraham Lincoln, who died on this date — April 15 — in 1865. What might have been an antiquarian courtroom drama or a belated eruption of Bush-era civil libertarian outrage has been given potent and painful currency by recent events.

headline.main: History’s Loose Ends, and a Tightening Noose

docs.snippet: “The Princess of Montpensier,” Bertrand Tavernier’s period tale about wars on the battlefield and those closer to home, is a rousing amalgam of ambition, moods and genre conceits.
docs.lead_paragraph: There are times when the lights are low and the bodices have been gently loosened that “The Princess of Montpensier,” a rousing amalgam of ambition, moods and genre conceits, looks like one of those old-fashioned diversions in which swords clang as bosoms heave with sweet passion. The pretty bosom of the title character played by Mélanie Thierry tends to swell rather gently, but it also rides so high in her dresses that it evokes the temptations displayed in the windows of Parisian patisseries. The French director Bertrand Tavernier deploys some smart ideas in this film, a period story about wars on the battlefield and those closer to home, but there’s something a bit goatish in his attention to some female charms.

docs.lead_paragraph: The history of modern war is also, in part, the history of the means by which war has been brought home to noncombatants. Certain conflicts became known through — and are now remembered by — specific image-making technologies. The Civil War is identified with the battlefield photographs of Mathew Brady and others; World War II coincided with the maturation of motion pictures; Vietnam came into American living rooms via television. In each case the specific properties of a given medium helped to shape public perception of the war and its effects.

docs.lead_paragraph: Lincoln’s Proclamation of April 15 is not a literary masterpiece. Nor was it trying to be. There was more urgent business to attend to — namely, the raising of 75,000 volunteers to defend Washington from attack. And yet, like every public document that issued from his pen, it is suffused with the particular phrasings of his mind. When seen in its handwritten version, below, courtesy of the Library of Congress, it is more clearly something that came from him, and not simply the great bureaucracy he personified as president. There are deletions, and inserts, and all the signs of a writer struggling to get it just right.

headline.main: Lincoln Declares War

Organized by Venus X Iceberg (née Jazmin Venus Soto), it serves as home base to many recently emerged hybrid rave/hip-hop genres. Soto is also producing a documentary called “Shakedown.” Reminiscent of the ’90s cult film “Paris Is Burning,” it traces the intricacies of black lesbian subculture in Los Angeles. Notably, Soto keeps her love of underground and subculture balanced. As a D.J., she has gained notoriety by mixing news clips from Al Jazeera in with her beats — during a New York Fashion Week gig, she interspersed coverage from the Egyptian revolution. As she puts it, “Even club kids should know what’s going on.”

docs.lead_paragraph: Every would-be writer needs comic books. I certainly did. I can still vividly recall my discovery of comic books, followed closely by the revelation that this reading stuff was actually good for something. Because comic books had it all over Readers. Comic books had pictures, and so did Readers, but in comic-book pictures somebody was flying or punching somebody, while in my Reader little Sally was crying about her little red boat. Even in my prepubescent days I had this vague feeling that Wonder Woman had it all over Jane, although I couldn’t put my finger on the reason. I did know that watching Spot run was a real drag when I could watch Krypto the Superdog fly instead. And I knew that if they ever met, Krypto would bite Spot’s head off.

docs.lead_paragraph: SOME great singing actors vanish into their characters. At the peak of his powers, the Welsh bass-baritone Bryn Terfel more typically swallows his alive. It happened in spades at the Metropolitan Opera a year ago when he joined the cast of Puccini’s “Tosca,” late in the run of the new, much-vilified production by Luc Bondy. As Baron Scarpia, the sadistic chief of the Roman police, Mr. Terfel captured the monster’s every facet, now in gallantries of silken delicacy, now in the savage bloodlust of a tiger on the attack. docs.lead_paragraph: Siddhartha Mukherjee has a terrific article in this Sunday’s magazine about whether cellphones cause cancer. When he’s not writing, Mukherjee does research and teaches medicine at Columbia University. That makes sense because reading his cellphone story feels a lot like sitting in a riveting college class, where the professor is leading you step by step through the history of what makes for excellent — as well as flawed — scientific research, all the while explaining how to assess the research on brain cancer and cellphones. Mukherjee’s writing is precise and vivid and you feel like you’re in the hands of a very thoughtful, exacting authority. Last fall the magazine published an excerpt from his recent book, “Emperor of All Maladies: A Biography of Cancer,” which was a finalist last year for the National Book Critics Circle Award and was named one of the 10-best books in 2010 by our Book Review.

docs.lead_paragraph: Near the end of his life, when he’d mostly given up lobbing oddball provocations at feminists and masturbators, Norman Mailer anointed “The Sopranos” as a cultural successor to the “great American novel.” It was a genuine compliment, though a strange one. Just as Mailer and Truman Capote once advertised the literary intentions of their journalism with the term “nonfiction novel,” Mailer now honored a television show by suggesting that it wasn’t a television show at all, but something else, something literary. The irony was that Mailer had it backward. “The Sopranos” represented the end of whatever remained of television’s status anxiety; it didn’t need to be anything but itself to be taken seriously.

docs.lead_paragraph: Kenji Yoshino is a respected legal scholar (the Chief Justice Earl Warren professor of constitutional law at New York University) who regularly teaches a course on literature and the law. The device he has come up with in “A Thousand Times More Fair” is to match a play of Shakespeare with some modern event or issue. One can see how this might stimulate class discussion, and it seems to succeed, since he tells us that his course on constitutional law is oversubscribed by two to one, but the class on literature and law has more applicants by six to one. The process apparently works. But what of the product? Considered apart from the give-and-take of the classroom, one of three things can be the result. First, the stereo­scopic approach can deepen one’s understanding of both a play and the event matched with it. Second, at least one of the pair can be given new understanding. Third, meaning can be drained, not deepened, on both sides of the matchup.

headline.main: Shakespeare Subpoenaed

docs.lead_paragraph: Assembling a collection of reviews and essays is a test of the richness of a critic’s inner life, an echo-sounding exercise that measures the depth of available talent. While a single piece may be impressive in isolation — rehearsed in a glossy magazine or nestled in the review pages — the book-length selection takes us out of the safety of those shallows and asks whether a writer’s reflections still rise beyond the threshold of banality when repeated over several hundred pages. If a critic’s sense of artistic achievement is sclerotically narrow, or based on a single approach applied to every work under consideration, the collection will coolly sketch a relief map of those failings.

docs.lead_paragraph: It’s not easy to pick the most unforgettable image from the many that flutter through this memoir like snippets from an overturned wastebasket. Susan Sontag eating a whole package of bacon and calling it dinner? Susan Sontag, passionate friend of the revolution, berating any clerk or waiter who didn’t treat her with proper deference? Susan Sontag perched on a sofa in her son’s room late at night, smoking and soliloquizing about her evening out, while he and his girlfriend lie silently in bed? Truly an embarrassment of riches, emphasis on the embarrassment, but here’s a personal favorite: Susan Sontag choosing to entertain guests in the kitchen.

docs.lead_paragraph: Diane Ackerman and Paul West have combined brilliant literary careers with the most enviable of marriages, a “decades-long duet.” Speculating on their longevity as a couple in “One Hundred Names for Love,” Ackerman writes: “We stayed together for the children — each was the other’s child. And we were both wordsmiths, cuddle-mad, and extremely playful. . . . All couples play kissy games they don’t want other people to know about, and all regress to infants from time to time, since, though we marry as adults, we don’t marry adults. We marry children who have grown up and still rejoice in being children, especially if we’re creative. Imaginative people fidget with ideas, including the idea of a relationship. If they’re wordsmiths like us, they fidget a lot in words.”

docs.lead_paragraph: Lydia Elkrunner (née Callahan) is not a very nice person. She insults on a whim and delights in temper tantrums. She refuses to repair the brake lights on her decaying BMW because that “would be giving other drivers too much information.” At 58, she acts as if she’s 20 and, of a benign nonagenarian, gleefully quips, “Don’t you admire the Eskimo ritual of leaving their elderly behind on an ice flow.” Really, she’s everything self: self-absorbed, self-important, self-indulgent. “You know why living with you would be so healthy, Grandma?” her down-and-out 28-year-old granddaughter remarks. “Because you are so incredibly wrong that you clarify what is right.”

docs.snippet: HBO’s drama “Cinema Verite” examines the making of the 1973 PBS documentary mini-series “An American Family,” examining the players on both sides of the camera.
docs.lead_paragraph: WHEN the documentary series “An American Family” was broadcast on PBS in 1973, critical and popular reaction varied, but many viewers, including prominent ones, agreed that it was a watershed of some kind. The anthropologist Margaret Mead proclaimed the show “as new and significant as the invention of drama or the novel.” For a host of commentators, conservatives and liberals alike, the series heralded nothing less than the demise of the nuclear family. Looking back on it in the 1980s, the philosopher Jean Baudrillard described “An American Family” as a symptom of our altered relationship with reality, characterized by “dissolution of TV in life, dissolution of life in TV.”

docs.abstract: Fashion is many things: beautiful, frivolous, devout, serious — sometimes all at once. It is performance and craft, in whatever style.
docs.snippet: Fashion is many things: beautiful, frivolous, devout, serious — sometimes all at once. It is performance and craft, in whatever style.
docs.lead_paragraph: Fashion is many things: beautiful, frivolous, devout, serious — sometimes all at once. It is performance and craft, in whatever style. In photographs and videos, it supplies us with visual intelligence. On May 2, when Daphne Guinness climbs into a window at Barneys New York to prepare for the Costume Institute gala that evening at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, I hope I have my own frock ready so I can go and watch. Do I think my friend is nutty? Yes, a little. Brave, definitely. And I am far from confident at this stage that anyone can create a performance-art piece with fashion that will mean anything, least of all in a luxury store window on Madison Avenue, and a time when apparel isn’t selling so well. But I’ll go anyway, just to see.

headline.main: Spring Theater of the Absurd

docs.lead_paragraph: The only thing clear about diamonds may be the translucent stones themselves. Everything else is murky and vaguely sinister: where they come from, who dug them up and under what conditions, and, more particularly, if they reek of evil. A diamond isn’t like fur, which can’t do much to hide its origins. But there is a lurking suspicion that, like the gold of the Nibelungs, no good can come from this bright rock. It doesn’t help that the one word that rushes unbidden to stand next to diamond is blood. Diamonds are guilty until proven innocent.

But not to be overlooked is our cover star, Cate Blanchett. She is well known, of course, for her portrayals of everyone from Queen Elizabeth I to Katharine Hepburn. In her new film, “Hanna,” she tries the role of ruthless C.I.A. agent on for size. But lesser known perhaps are the slew of roles she plays off-screen, including the co-artistic director of the Sydney Theater Company, an eco-activist who works with the Australian Conservation Foundation and the mother of three young boys. docs.abstract: Twelve years after “Mad About You,” Paul Reiser made a low-rated return to NBC’s comedy line-up on Thursday.
docs.snippet: Twelve years after “Mad About You,” Paul Reiser made a low-rated return to NBC’s comedy line-up on Thursday.
docs.lead_paragraph: Twelve years after “Mad About You,” Paul Reiser made a low-rated return to NBC’s comedy line-up on Thursday. Just 3.3 million viewers tuned in to the premiere of “The Paul Reiser Show” at 8:30 p.m., according to Nielsen’s estimates. The new series faces considerable odds, coming after NBC’s similarly ratings-starved sitcom “Community” (3.5 million), at 8 p.m., and occupying a time slot otherwise dominated by “American Idol” on Fox. For the night, NBC ranked a distant third, garnering its best ratings at 9 p.m. for “The Office” (7.7 million), which featured a guest appearance from Will Ferrell. Fox led the night with 21 million viewers tuning for an elimination episode of “Idol” and 11.9 million at 9 p.m. for “Bones.” CBS placed second, despite broadcasting a line-up of all repeats. ABC was fourth, finishing close behind NBC with reruns from 9 to 11 p.m. following a new episode of “Wipeout” at 8 (6.2 million).

headline.main: Viewers Not So Mad About Paul Reiser’s Return

docs.abstract: This was one of those magical weeks of bedtime reading, when the house got perfectly quiet and my books got very loud and I ended up staying up until 2 in the morning just about every night.
docs.snippet: This was one of those magical weeks of bedtime reading, when the house got perfectly quiet and my books got very loud and I ended up staying up until 2 in the morning just about every night.
docs.lead_paragraph: This was one of those magical weeks of bedtime reading, when the house got perfectly quiet and my books got very loud and I ended up staying up until 2 in the morning just about every night. I was reading: a big, heavy, three-volume hardcover edition of Samuel Johnson’s “Lives of the Poets”; a newfangled iPhone essay (with pictures, audio, etc.) about ants called “Before the Swarm”; “Father and Son,” Edmund Gosse’s 1907 memoir about growing up with evangelical Christian parents (this was also on my iPhone, via the less high-tech Project Gutenberg); and an advance copy of Nicholson Baker’s erotic fantasy novel “House of Holes: A Book of Raunch.” (This won’t be published until August, but — hoo-boy, people, get ready for this book. It is going to be Talked About. There will be fistfights in the hallways of your local public library. I keep describing it to people as “porny Alice in Wonderland” — an impossible combination of crazy, cheerful imagination and industrial-grade filth. It made me hoot out loud every other page or so, and on a few occasions my mouth actually, literally dropped open. Just get ready.)

headline.main: Sentence of the Week, Insomnia Edition

docs.lead_paragraph: A few weeks ago, colleges and universities notified millions of restless high school seniors of their admissions decisions for fall 2011. In an environment that becomes more competitive year after year, we asked a sampling of colleges and universities for a sense of how things were stacking up. Over all, admittance rates continued to decline. For example, the Ivy League on average admitted 10 percent of applicants, down from the 11 percent recorded last year. The results shouldn’t surprise. Some 2.2 million online applications have been filed for the fall using the Common Application alone, up almost 22 percent from 2010. The glut of applications means admissions offices must deny an increasing proportion of students. But take heart: when the dust settled on last fall’s freshmen class, the average acceptance rate was 67 percent.

docs.lead_paragraph: Back in early 2002, when Gary Taubes was writing a cover story called “What If It’s All Been a Big Fat Lie?” for this magazine, he and I had lunch every couple of months at Les Deux Gamins, a cafe in the West Village. At the time, I was one of those normal people who ate Cheerios for breakfast, but all that changed as I got to know Gary better. My lunches with him were like meetings with a parole officer, only it wasn’t a life of crime that Gary was steering me away from — it was a life of carbohydrates. The first time we went to Les Deux Gamins, the waitress offered us a bread basket. She never did again.

docs.lead_paragraph: My first, most vivid television memory is of watching the Watergate hearings in 1973 at my rapt mother’s side. My second involves exposure to villainy of another kind — that of Billy Clyde Tuggle, the sort of pimp who drugged his employee base on “All My Children.” For these encounters with Tuggle, my mother was absent. She was then, and remains now, in her late 80s, a largely “news only, no sap, thank you” participant in the experience of American television. She reserved (and reserves) her greatest disdain for soap opera “drivel” and, inevitably perhaps, my addiction to daytime television became my most impassioned act of adolescent subversion.

Students at Makerere University threw stones at the police and burned kiosks as officers shot rubber bullets and threw tear-gas canisters, above, into dormitories and fleeing crowds. The protest began over a report that university administrators planned to double the tuition, which the administration denied, but turned into a protest against President Yoweri Museveni. There have been several small protests over the last week against rising prices and corruption. Protests were also reported in the west on Friday. On Thursday, a former presidential candidate and leading opposition figure, Kizza Besigye, was shot during street demonstrations in Kampala, the capital.

headline.main: Uganda: Antigovernment Protest Set Off by Tuition-Increase Report

docs.abstract: At least 54 people have been detained in the current crackdown on progressive thought and speech, according to a statement released by China Human Rights Defenders.
docs.snippet: At least 54 people have been detained in the current crackdown on progressive thought and speech, according to a statement released by China Human Rights Defenders.
docs.lead_paragraph: At least 54 people have been detained in the current crackdown on progressive thought and speech in China, according to a statement released Thursday by China Human Rights Defenders, an advocacy group. The latest person to be detained is Ni Yulan, a housing activist and former lawyer, after previously being tortured by security officers. Ms. Ni and her husband, Dong Jiqin, were taken on April 7 from a Beijing hotel where they had been living. Ms. Ni has not been charged with a crime. So far, four people have been criminally charged during the crackdown. Ms. Ni is likely to have come under increased scrutiny after Jon Huntsman Jr., the American ambassador, visited her in February. Mr. Huntsman and the United States government are suspected by some Chinese officials of promoting the calls for a so-called Jasmine Revolution to challenge Communist Party rule. The most famous of the 54 detainees is Ai Weiwei, an artist and democracy activist.

headline.main: China: 54 Detained in Crackdown
headline.print_headline: China: 54 Detained in Crackdown

Two-thirds of bachelor’s degree recipients graduated with debt in 2008, compared with less than half in 1993. Overall, student loan debt outpaced credit card debt for the first time last year and is likely to top a trillion dollars this year as more students go to college and more borrow money to do so. “In the coming years, a lot of people will still be paying off their student loans when it’s time for their kids to go to college,” Mr. Kantrowitz said.

docs.lead_paragraph: The conductor Riccardo Muti has always had a big following in New York. So it was no surprise that Carnegie Hall was sold out for Friday night’s concert performance of Verdi’s “Otello,” the first of Mr. Muti’s three programs with the Chicago Symphony Orchestra. His hugely anticipated first season as this historic orchestra’s music director has been twice interrupted for extended periods in recent months by serious health crises. But worries about his health vanished on Friday as Mr. Muti, looking calm, fit and rather self-satisfied, conducted an emphatic and insightful account of this challenging Verdi opera, drawing incisive and beautiful playing from the orchestra.

docs.lead_paragraph: Hollywood’s parade of cartoon hits continues: “Rio,” above, was No. 1 at North American theaters over the weekend with an estimated $40 million in ticket sales. The tale of a Minnesota macaw on the hunt for love in South America, “Rio” cost 20th Century Fox about $90 million to make — cheaper than many animated films — and has already caught on overseas, where ticket sales total about $128 million. “Scream 4,” which cost the Weinstein Company about $40 million to make, was second with $19.3 million. That result was 57 percent less than the opening weekend in 2000 for the last installment of the “Scream” franchise, after adjusting for inflation. (But Weinstein does not have to split any profits with Disney, as it did on the previous “Scream” films.) “Hop,” from Universal Pictures, was third with about $11.2 million for a three-week total of $82.6 million, according to Hollywood.com, which compiles box-office statistics. “Soul Surfer” (Sony) was fourth with $7.4 million for a two-week total of about $20 million. “Hanna” (Focus Features) was fifth with about $7.3 million for a two-week total of $23.3 million. Also notable: Robert Redford’s “Conspirator” (Roadside Attractions) sold $3.9 million in tickets in limited release.

headline.main: ‘Rio’ Takes Top Spot at Weekend Box Office
headline.print_headline: ‘Rio’ Takes Top Spot At Weekend Box Office

docs.abstract: The fall exhibition at the Cooper-Hewitt National Design is focused on design solutions to the problems of global slums.
docs.snippet: The fall exhibition at the Cooper-Hewitt National Design is focused on design solutions to the problems of global slums.
docs.lead_paragraph: Remodeling can be inconvenient, particularly for museums. But the Cooper-Hewitt National Design Museum, faced with the coming renovation of its historic mansion at Fifth Avenue and 91st Street, below, has found a not-inappropriate spot for its fall exhibition, which is focused on design solutions to the problems of global slums. The museum is to announce on Monday that the exhibition, titled “Design With the Other 90%: Cities,” will be at the United Nations. The second of two similarly themed exhibitions, the show will feature roughly 60 projects from 20 countries, aimed at solving problems related to housing, access to clean water, education, waste management and transportation. It will run from Oct. 15 to Jan. 9, and admission will be free. The mansion renovation is part of a $54 million overhaul that will create 6,000 square feet of new gallery space, a new library and additional classrooms for the museum’s master’s program. The museum will reopen in 2013.

headline.main: United Nations to Host Cooper-Hewitt Show
headline.print_headline: United Nations to Host Cooper-Hewitt Show

docs.lead_paragraph: An Egyptian criminal court on Sunday sentenced Egypt’s antiquities minister, Zahi Hawass, to a year in jail and ordered him removed from his job, Ahram Online, the English language Web site of the Egyptian state newspaper, reported. The sentence arose out of a dispute over the assigning of a contract to run a bookstore at the Egyptian museum, said Farid Atiya, who sued Mr. Hawass in that dispute. By e-mail, Mr. Hawass denied that he was going to jail and said that the antiquities ministry would file an appeal in the case on Monday. Mr. Atiya, who ran a bookstore next to the museum from 2004 to 2010, said that the verdict would be set aside if Mr. Hawass, within 10 days, closed a new bookstore and gift shop, affiliated with the American University in Cairo Press, that Mr. Atiya said had been opened in violation of a court order. Mr. Hawass, who had long been Egypt’s top antiquities official, resigned in March and was reinstated two weeks ago.

headline.main: Antiquities Official Sentenced in Egypt

docs.lead_paragraph: Though only read once or twice a year, it has probably had more wine spilled on it than any other book ever published. docs.abstract: Kundera was showing us not only how one major event sweeps away another, but just how hard it is to remember at all, how disorienting to our own point of view and sense of time it is to try to follow what is going on around us.
docs.snippet: Kundera was showing us not only how one major event sweeps away another, but just how hard it is to remember at all, how disorienting to our own point of view and sense of time it is to try to follow what is going on around us.
docs.lead_paragraph: When I was a junior in high school, I became obsessed with the Czech novelist Milan Kundera. I would apologize for my pretentiousness, except that it is still an essential part of who I am. I copied a passage from “The Book of Laughter and Forgetting” onto the first divider in my loose-leaf notebook and tried to get as many of my classmates as I could to check it out. This was not no one, but it wasn’t a tremendous number of people either. Repeated reading dug the passage into my mind, and the other day when I was thinking about how hard it is to keep up with the violent pace at which so-called current events are overturning each other worldwide, it popped up unasked for:

headline.main: Remembering and Forgetting Milan Kundera

docs.lead_paragraph: In the pantheon of fantasy and science-fiction projects that Joss Whedon helped create, the Internet musical “Dr. Horrible’s Sing-Along Blog” can be easy to overlook: it’s not his beloved television series that ran a healthy seven seasons (“Buffy the Vampire Slayer”), or its beloved spinoff (“Angel”), or his misunderstood television show that was canceled before its time (“Dollhouse”) or his other misunderstood television show that was canceled before its time and spawned a misunderstood movie (“Firefly” and “Serenity”). “Dr. Horrible” is simply a three-act musical about an aspiring super-villain (played by Neil Patrick Harris), his smug do-gooding nemesis (Nathan Fillion) and the woman who comes between them (Felicia Day). Dreamed up by Mr. Whedon, his brothers Zack and Jed, and Maurissa Tancharoen during the 2007-8 writers’ strike and produced on his own dime, it is the pure expression of what they wanted to make at the time, without any outside interference.

headline.main: Once More, With Feeling: Joss Whedon Revisits ‘Dr. Horrible’s Sing-Along Blog’

Today all the saw mills are gone, and so are their jobs. Three years ago, Les Schwab, the town’s best-known business, moved its headquarters to nearby Bend, taking with it about 100 well-paying jobs. In the last 18 months, more than 1,000 residents left the town and the county, which has the highest rate of unemployment in Oregon at roughly 20 percent.

headline.main: Facebook and Prineville, Ore., Become Friends

docs.abstract: Why the figure cited in today’s column seems so high.
docs.snippet: Why the figure cited in today’s column seems so high.
docs.lead_paragraph: My column today includes an estimate, taken from this Congressional Budget Office report, of what a median-income family would pay in taxes over the next few decades under the “current law baseline” — a scenario in which tax rates rise fast enough to cover the budget deficit without any kind of entitlement reform. The median income figure the C.B.O. used (see Table 4-4 on p. 65 of the report) is $94,900 for a family of four, which (as a number of readers have noted) seems much higher than the usual estimates for median income in a four-person household. It turns out that I didn’t catch a crucial footnote in the C.B.O. document: “All income is assumed to be from compensation, which includes employment-based health insurance and the employer’s share of payroll taxes.” That is to say, the $94,900 in income includes the estimated value of the median family’s health care plan as well as their salary, which is not what most people think of when they hear the term “median income.” I apologize for the confusion.

headline.main: A Note on Median Income

docs.lead_paragraph: Even among the Warhol Superstars, Candy Darling was a standout. Her spot-on embodiment of a ’40s-era Hollywood starlet — demure, mysterious, quiet — stood in contrast to the pretty-little-rich-girl routine of Edie Sedgwick, the drug-fueled silver-tongued cheek of Brigid Berlin and the Teutonic otherness of Nico. And the fact that she was a transgendered woman from Long Island only added to her mystique. Her fame spread via the Paul Morrissey films “Flesh” and “Women in Revolt,” and she was immortalized by Lou Reed in the songs “Candy Says” and “Walk on the Wild Side.” She died in 1974, from leukemia connected to unsafe hormone treatments, at the age of 29.

headline.main: Eye Candy

ABC ranked close behind CBS in second place for the night, leading during the 9 p.m. hour with “Desperate Housewives” (8.8 million). NBC placed third over all, garnering an average of 7.4 million viewers for “The Celebrity Apprentice” from 9 to 11. Fox was fourth with its animated comedy lineup, although “Family Guy” (6 million) earned the night’s highest ratings in the demographic of adults 18 to 49.

docs.lead_paragraph: For the third season in a row, the Metropolitan Opera is offering recitals instead of full-scale operas for its free summer parks series. The Met announced in a statement on Monday that the soprano Angela Meade, the mezzo-soprano Jennifer Johnson Cano and the tenor Dimitri Pittas would perform on July 11 in Central Park and on July 13 in Brooklyn Bridge Park. Three other singers would present programs in Crotona Park in the Bronx (July 19); Clove Lakes Park on Staten Island (July 21); Socrates Sculpture Park in Long Island City, Queens (July 26); and Jackie Robinson Park in Harlem (July 28). Those performers will be Layla Claire, a soprano; Renée Tatum, a mezzo-soprano; and Ryan Speedo Green, a bass-baritone. The pianist Bradley Moore will be the accompanist for all of the concerts. The statement said the Met would also present free outdoor screenings of its high-definition broadcasts from Lincoln Center from Aug. 27 to Sept. 5. The last full Met opera in the park was in the summer of 2007. In 2008, the Met presented a lone recital by the soprano Angela Gheorghiu and the tenor Roberto Alagna.

docs.lead_paragraph: I hadn’t really watched “All My Children” on a daily basis since 2004, when Bianca Montgomery, Erica Kane’s lesbian daughter, finally discovered that Miranda, the baby she thought had died in an accident, was actually Bess, the baby her best friend, Babe, was passing off as her own. Around the same period, I also stopped watching “One Life to Live” regularly, following the heart transplant that Victoria Lord Riley Burke Riley Buchanan Buchanan Carpenter Davidson received thanks to the untimely death of the love of her life and sixth husband, Ben, who lay comatose in a hospital bed for months after being accidentally shot in the head during an attempt to save Viki from a kidnapper. Still, I was taken aback by last week’s news that after more than 40 years of showing them five days a week, 52 weeks a year, ABC was axing both shows, one by September and the other by January 2012, leaving just “The Young and the Restless,” “The Bold and the Beautiful,” “Days of Our Lives” and “General Hospital” to carry on the daytime-serial legacy.

docs.abstract: We’re going to go find a cash machine while we wait for the late summer release of Jeff Bridges’s solo album for Blue Note Records.
docs.snippet: We’re going to go find a cash machine while we wait for the late summer release of Jeff Bridges’s solo album for Blue Note Records.
docs.lead_paragraph: When the Dude sought recreation in “The Big Lebowski,” he’d bowl, drive around, enjoy the occasional acid flashback and unwind to some Creedence Clearwater Revival. Now it’s C.C.R.’s turn to unwind to the Dude. Jeff Bridges, the “Big Lebowski” star who played a country singer so well in “Crazy Heart” he won an Academy Award for it, will record a solo album for the Blue Note Records division of EMI, the label said on Tuesday. The album, which does not yet have a title (can we humbly suggest “Careful, Man, There’s A Beverage Here”?) will be recorded with the producer T-Bone Burnett, who first met Mr. Bridges on the set of “Heaven’s Gate,” and selected music for the “Big Lebowski” soundtrack and co-wrote songs for “Crazy Heart,” including the Oscar-nominated track “The Weary Kind.” Blue Note Records said in a statement that Mr. Bridges “will contribute several of his own compositions” and perform songs by Stephen Bruton and John Goodwin, Greg Brown, Bo Ramsey, Tom Waits, and others. Though we wouldn’t hold out much hope for the Dude’s Creedence cassettes, Mr. Bridges’s album is planned for a late summer release.

headline.main: The Dude Records: Jeff Bridges Plans Solo Album

ABC easily led the night over all despite a diminished audience after the dancing competition for its sitcom “Cougar Town” at 9:30 (8.5 million). CBS’s “Hawaii Five-0” led at 10 p.m., drawing 10.9 million viewers and outperforming ABC’s “20/20” special (7.6 million). CBS ranked second, earning modest ratings for its comedy lineup from 8 to 10, including “How I Met Your Mother” (6.4 million), “Mad Love” (5.6 million) and “Mike & Molly” (9.7 million), while a repeat of “Two and a Half Men” attracted 7.3 million viewers at 9. Fox was third with “House” at 8 (8.6 million) and “The Chicago Code” at 9 (6.4 million). NBC struggled in fourth place with “Chuck” (4.2 million) and “The Event” (3.7 million) followed by the recently rebooted version of “Law & Order: Los Angeles” (4.9 million).

headline.main: ‘Dancing With the Stars’ Dominates Ratings for ABC

docs.lead_paragraph: If the equivalent of an Academy Award were offered for best performance as a muse to artists, Marie-Thérèse Walter would surely have won one. She was 17 years old in 1927, when she met a strangely charismatic, short man with mesmerizing eyes, sporting a handsome red-and-black striped tie, on the sidewalk outside the Galeries Lafayette department store in Paris, where she’d gone to buy a Peter Pan collar and cuffs. “You have an interesting face,” he told her. “I’d like to do your portrait.” The name Picasso meant nothing to her, but she kept the appointment they made at his studio the next day, igniting a passion that would change the course of his art.

headline.main: Just Looking | ‘L’Amour Fou’

docs.lead_paragraph: Belarus announced Tuesday that it would allow its flagging currency to trade freely between banks, all but ensuring a devaluation of the ruble in an effort to ease an increasingly dire economic situation. The exchange rate had previously been fixed. Economists have said that the move would help jump-start the economy by lowering prices on exports, slowing the outflow of dollars and euros. But the decision will probably cause inflation to spike, further undermining confidence in Belarus’s authoritarian president, Aleksandr G. Lukashenko. Soviet-style economic policies have depleted Belarus’s foreign currency reserves, and people have been waiting in long lines to exchange rubles for increasingly scarce dollars and euros. The sense of crisis was compounded last week by a bombing at a subway station in the capital, Minsk, that killed 13 people.

headline.main: Belarus: Currency to Be Traded
headline.print_headline: Belarus: Currency to Be Traded

At a meeting in Vientiane, the Laotian capital, officials from Laos, Thailand, Cambodia and Vietnam postponed a decision on the Xayaburi dam, which would be the first across the Mekong south of the Chinese border. The dam is the first in a series of large-scale hydroelectric projects on the Mekong that the cash-strapped Laotian government is pursuing in order to sell electricity to other countries. Cambodia and Thailand recommended further studies of the dam’s environmental impact, and Vietnam, which fears deleterious effects to the Mekong Delta, called for a moratorium on dams across the Mekong. The governments did not say when they would meet to decide the issue.

docs.abstract: In 1967, Stanley Ann Dunham took her 6-year-old son, Barry, on an adventure, transplanting him to Indonesia. She did not know just how much it would change her life, and his.
docs.snippet: In 1967, Stanley Ann Dunham took her 6-year-old son, Barry, on an adventure, transplanting him to Indonesia. She did not know just how much it would change her life, and his.
docs.lead_paragraph: The photograph showed the son, but my eye gravitated toward the mother. That first glimpse was surprising — the stout, pale-skinned woman in sturdy sandals, standing squarely a half-step ahead of the lithe, darker-skinned figure to her left. His elas­tic-band body bespoke discipline, even asceticism. Her form was well padded, territory ceded long ago to the pleasures of appetite and the forces of anatomical destiny. He had the studied casualness of a catalog model, in khakis, at home in the viewfinder. She met the camera head-on, dressed in hand-loomed textile dyed indigo, a silver earring half-hidden in the cascading curtain of her dark hair. She carried her chin a few degrees higher than most. His right hand rested on her shoulder, lightly. The photograph, taken on a Manhattan rooftop in August 1987 and e-mailed to me 20 years later, was a revelation and a puzzle. The man was Barack Obama at 26, the community organizer from Chicago on a visit to New York. The woman was Stanley Ann Dunham, his mother. It was impossible not to be struck by the similarities, and the dissimilarities, between them. It was impossible not to question the stereotype to which she had been expediently reduced: the white woman from Kansas.

headline.main: Obama’s Young Mother Abroad
headline.print_headline: THE YOUNG MOTHER ABROAD

docs.lead_paragraph: As a rule, digging beneath the surface of modern Rome turns up ancient buildings. Excavations conducted in 2007, just steps from the traffic hub of Piazza Venezia, revealed two Imperial era villas embellished with mosaics, polychrome wall veneers, fountains and frescoes. docs.lead_paragraph: I’m currently learning how to knit, but I’m still at the stage where offering to make someone anything is more a threat than a favor. After looking around online this weekend for tutorials and patterns, I stumbled across a video about Althea Crome and was amazed at the amount of detail that goes into her miniature creations. The most recognizable pieces in her collection are the starred sweater and mittens that the title character wears in the 2009 animated film “Coraline,” from the animation studio Laika. docs.abstract: The annual celebration of arts in lower Manhattan will feature Philip Glass, Laurie Anderson, Patti Smith, Rufus Wainwright, Sean Lennon and Rosanne Cash, as well as a two-castle production of “Henry V.”
docs.snippet: The annual celebration of arts in lower Manhattan will feature Philip Glass, Laurie Anderson, Patti Smith, Rufus Wainwright, Sean Lennon and Rosanne Cash, as well as a two-castle production of “Henry V.”
docs.lead_paragraph: Downtown mainstays including Philip Glass, Laurie Anderson, Patti Smith, Rufus Wainwright and Sean Lennon, and – straight from the Battle of Agincourt – Henry V will all be part of the 10th River to River Festival, the annual celebration of arts in lower Manhattan, its organizers said on Wednesday. The festival of free events, which runs from June 19 through July 16, will begin with the Bang on a Can Marathon at the World Financial Center Winter Garden, with performances by Mr. Glass, top, with the Bang on a Can All-Stars. The Castle Clinton National Monument in Battery Park will host concerts featuring Vijay Iyer (on June 23); Ms. Anderson, above, with Bill Laswell (June 30); and Ms. Smith (July 14). Rockefeller Park will be the setting of a June 22 tribute to the Bottom Line, featuring Rosanne Cash, Dar Williams and Marshall Crenshaw. Mr. Wainwright and soloists from the New York City Opera will perform excerpts from his opera “Prima Donna” at the World Financial Center Winter Garden on June 28. Mr. Lennon’s band the Ghost of a Saber Tooth Tiger will perform at the Seaport on June 24. And New York Classical Theater will present a two-castle production of Shakespeare‘s “Henry V” at Castle Clinton in Battery Park and Castle William on Governors Island (with free ferry service between the locations). A complete schedule and other information can be found at the festival’s Web site, rivertorivernyc.com.

headline.main: River to River Festival Announces Lineup

docs.lead_paragraph: We are not just eating a steak, or an omelet, when our fork lands, tines down, into our food. We, as conscious consumers, are eating all of the resources it took to raise that cow and transport those eggs from farm to fork. So, as trends go, it is somewhat encouraging, if not a bit beguiling, to see such a rudimentary ingredient as hay (yes, plain old barnyard hay) begin to appear on menus around the country, as well as Europe. We have effectively cut out the middleman (the ruminant cow) and gone straight to the pasture.

headline.main: First We Eat | Hitting the Hay

docs.snippet: The Coach Classics collection revives the company’s classic Duffle — just the sort of no-logo, no-hardware, no-nonsense bag that no one is making anymore.
docs.lead_paragraph: The Coach Duffle bag, which was designed in the 1970s by Bonnie Cashin, is just the sort of no-logo, no-hardware, no-nonsense bag that no one is making anymore. Not even Coach, which saw fit to put this workhorse out to pasture in 1997. But starting June 15, Net-a-Porter is bringing back the Duffle, as well as four other seminal styles from that era, as the Coach Classics collection. Fans of the original will notice only one minor adjustment: an ad for Neiman Marcus in The Dallas Morning News from the ’70s listed the Duffle for $36. This summer it will set you back $398.

docs.lead_paragraph: There’s no disputing the socialite bona fides of Maggie Betts, the daughter of the film producer and Chelsea Piers developer Roland Betts and a fixture of Gotham’s party scene. But Betts, a 36-year-old Princeton graduate, is also a passionate advocate for AIDS awareness in Africa who has spent long periods on the continent bearing witness to the epidemic. Her first film, “The Carrier,” which premieres Thursday as part of the Tribeca Film Festival, is the culmination of five years of research. The documentary tells the story of a Zambian woman, Mutinta Mweemba, who tries desperately not to pass on her HIV infection to her unborn child. Here, Betts is interviewed by the designer Prabal Gurung, her good friend and the recently appointed Goodwill Ambassador for the nonprofit group Maiti Nepal.

docs.lead_paragraph: An interesting discussion, but this type of article only feeds our obsession with esoteric and unusual conditions. Medical journals and popular TV shows are full of these types of examples. There’s a common saying: When you hear hoof beats, think horses, not zebras. Unfortunately, doctors and the lay public are automatically thinking zebras as a first reaction. What’s the worst-case scenario? What test can we order to rule out a tumor, growth or genetic mutation? It’s a sad state of affairs when we can’t even manage the most basic medical conditions properly, while glorifying rare and unusual conditions.

docs.abstract: A reunited Big Audio Dynamite tries to give new context to its 1980s hits.
docs.snippet: A reunited Big Audio Dynamite tries to give new context to its 1980s hits.
docs.lead_paragraph: In the mid-1980s Big Audio Dynamite latched onto good ideas early. From its home in London, where its leader, Mick Jones, had been a punk-rock pioneer with the Clash in the 1970s, Big Audio Dynamite checked out club music from across the Atlantic: South Bronx hip-hop, Jamaican dub reggae, Detroit techno, Chicago house. It mingled drum machines and rock guitar, adding synthesizers and samples, with Mr. Jones singing and Don Letts sometimes rapping or toasting, Jamaican-style. Their fractured lyrics took up politics, music, multiculturalism and self-affirmation. If the term hipster had been tossed around the way it is now, Big Audio Dynamite would easily have qualified.

docs.lead_paragraph: A prominent independent documentary film festival in China, scheduled this year for May, has been canceled because of the tense atmosphere created by the continuing government crackdown on freedom of speech. The English edition of Global Times, a populist newspaper, published an article on Wednesday about the cancellation in which it quoted Zhu Rikun, the festival’s art director, saying the organizers had decided to cancel it themselves. “The overall situation was tense, and we had received a lot of pressure,” Mr. Zhu said. “We worried that the films to be shown would meet some problems in this environment and decided to cancel it.” Another festival organizer, Li Shanshan, told Global Times that about 20 overseas guests, 10 directors and around 40 fans had registered to attend the festival. The cancellation of the festival, which is usually held every year in Songzhuang, on the outskirts of Beijing, was first announced Monday on the festival’s microblog on sina.com.

headline.main: China: Documentary Film Festival Is Canceled
headline.print_headline: China: Documentary Film Festival Is Canceled

docs.abstract: A look at the Peter Lindbergh and Diane Von Furstenberg exhibitions now on view in the Chinese capital.
docs.snippet: A look at the Peter Lindbergh and Diane Von Furstenberg exhibitions now on view in the Chinese capital.
docs.lead_paragraph: Two of the best art shows in Beijing at the moment aren’t necessarily the newest. “The Unknown,” which opened April 1 (at the tail end of China Fashion Week) at the Ullens Center for Contemporary Art, is the fashion photographer Peter Lindbergh’s first solo exhibition in China. “The Unknown” is not a Lindbergh retrospective,” says the museum’s director, Jerome Sans, “but a body of work specifically assembled to mark his first experience with China.” A gigantic remix without order or chronology, the installation is a visual journey through decades of the photographer’s career, including photos of supermodels like Naomi Campbell, Christy Turlington and Linda Evangelista, most of which were commissioned for Italian Vogue by Franca Sozzani (who was present for the opening). Visitors enter the exhibition in a space surrounded by video images from Lindbergh’s recent cinematic series, “Invasion,” a film that depicts a crowd in slow motion moving into a cloud of smoke. Visitors to the exhibit suddenly realize they have become part of the silent choreography, as they watch their own shadows entering and exiting the images projected onto the walls.

headline.main: T in China | Art and Fashion in Beijing

docs.abstract: “Home Show, Revisited,” opening this month at the Santa Barbara Contemporary Arts Forum in California, puts a new spin on the expression “mi casa, su casa.”
docs.snippet: “Home Show, Revisited,” opening this month at the Santa Barbara Contemporary Arts Forum in California, puts a new spin on the expression “mi casa, su casa.”
docs.lead_paragraph: “Home Show, Revisited,” opening this month at the Santa Barbara Contemporary Arts Forum in California, puts a new spin on the expression “mi casa, su casa.” Now in its third iteration, the site-specific exhibition pairs 10 Los Angeles artists with 9 area residences, inviting the artists to explore the notion of home. Some of the work, like the circular swimming pool that Piero Golia built in the yard of an updated Spanish-style gem or Jennifer West’s experimental surf films, which will screen at sundown at a Carpinteria surf shack, makes direct references to life in Southern California. Other installations play with personal space: the sculptor Ry Rocklen’s tiled floor piece speaks to the work of the mosaic artist who is hosting him, and Bettina Hubby (above) has created curtains — depicting her “living” inside a Montecito Tudor — that will hang outside the windows, “providing privacy for the owners but exposing me,” she says. For info on self-guided tours, go to sbcaf.org.

headline.main: Space Invaders

docs.abstract: The Lyric Opera of Chicago has named a new general director, Anthony Freud.
docs.snippet: The Lyric Opera of Chicago has named a new general director, Anthony Freud.
docs.lead_paragraph: The Lyric Opera of Chicago has named a new general director, Anthony Freud, who has been running the Houston Grand Opera for the past five years. Mr. Freud, 53, will take over in the fall for William Mason, 69, the general director since 1997, who said in July he would retire after this season. Mr. Freud, a onetime record company executive and former chairman of the jury for the BBC Cardiff Singer of the World Competition, ran the Welsh National Opera before coming to Houston in 2006. A Londoner, he has become a key insider in the American opera world and is chairman of the Opera America service organization. If you fear for his arteries, you can check out an analysis of his blood lipids posted on his blog. When I talked to Gary this morning, he was in Los Angeles, visiting family for spring break, and (in addition to answering hundreds of sugar-related e-mails) was preparing breakfast: scrambled eggs and bacon for his wife; scrambled eggs, bacon, Italian sausage and black coffee for himself; Cheerios, raisins and Italian sausage for the kids. docs.abstract: The young artist Brendan Dugan is making his presence known with Karma, a tiny graphic design bookstore in New York.
docs.snippet: The young artist Brendan Dugan is making his presence known with Karma, a tiny graphic design bookstore in New York.
docs.lead_paragraph: Pick up a book about a young New York artist these days, and you’re likely to spot Brendan Dugan’s name in the fine print. As the founder of the graphics firm and indie publishing imprint An Art Service, Dugan has become a go-to designer for galleries like Gagosian and Hauser & Wirth, or for virtually anyone in Dan Colen’s crowd. Now he’s slowly making his presence known with Karma (21 Downing Street; open Thursday-Sunday from noon to 7 p.m. or by appointment), a tiny shop in the front of his office where he sells his own catalog of gritty pop-minimalist art books and posters alongside books and objects that inspire him. Dugan started the publishing arm of his business in 2009 as an additional platform for the artists whose Web sites, books and ephemera he was already designing. “Allan Kaprow, Ed Ruscha and a lot of the Fluxus artists were designing all these amazing objects to help support their projects,” he says. “I guess I think of us as trying to help continue that lineage.”
