docs.snippet: Francine Prose’s wry novel of a young Albanian immigrant in New Jersey sets America in high relief, mordant and comic, light and dark.
docs.lead_paragraph: The great grinning tradition of American satire has always been healthy because this confounding country provides an abundance of jaw-dropping moments every day, moments that don’t need rewriting or amplification to reveal their comic craziness. All you need is the ability to see them and then present them plainly, as if you were born yesterday, with nothing but big eyes and a sense of right and wrong. O.K., maybe born the day before yesterday and in Albania, but still with that sense of right and wrong. Francine Prose has just such a sharp protagonist in her wry novel, “My New American Life,” a book that brims with smart surprises.

docs.abstract: While her husband pursues an affair, this sprightly novel’s heroine becomes immersed in an all-female world.
docs.snippet: While her husband pursues an affair, this sprightly novel’s heroine becomes immersed in an all-female world.
docs.lead_paragraph: One little word — “pause” — sets off the chain of events in which Mia Fredricksen, the 55-year-old poet and professor who narrates Siri Hust­vedt’s fifth novel, retreats for the summer to the “backwater” Minnesota town where she grew up. Her husband, a neuroscientist named Boris Izcovich, has asked for a “pause” in their marriage so he can take up with a younger colleague, “a woman with whom he had no past.” After a short, agonizing stay in a psychiatric ward, Mia decamps from her Brooklyn apartment to tiny Bonden, seeing no choice but to wait out the “cruel crack of hope” in her husband’s request. There she finds herself immersed, somewhat accidentally, in an all-female world that includes her mother’s five lively geriatric friends, the seven adolescent members of a poetry workshop and the young mother next door, whose husband travels often for work. Over the course of the summer, Mia confronts, with the help of phone sessions with her (female) therapist, her own history as a willing second-class citizen, “a scribbler of the stolen interval” who “hadn’t fought for myself.” Along the way, she re-examines everything she’s believed about the differences between men and women and the possibility of married love.

headline.main: Retreating From a Ruptured Marriage

docs.snippet: “Rhapsody,” Jennifer Bartlett’s epic polymorphous post-painting painting in nearly 1,000 parts, is again  on view at the Museum of Modern Art, wrapped around and looking tailor-made for the three long walls of the institution’s giant atrium.
docs.lead_paragraph: “Rhapsody,” Jennifer Bartlett’s epic polymorphous post-painting painting in nearly 1,000 parts is once again on view at the Museum of Modern Art, wrapped around three long walls and looking tailor-made for the museum’s giant atrium. The work was first shown here five years ago, as part of an exhibition of works given to the Modern by the collector Edward R. Broida. At that time, the piece’s appearance was an early indication that the atrium might serve as something other than a large, alienating event space.

headline.main: Jennifer Bartlett’s Epic ‘Rhapsody’ Back on View at the Modern

docs.lead_paragraph: As Michael Scott (Steve Carell) said goodbye on “The Office” on Thursday, the NBC sitcom delivered Thursday night’s second-highest ratings among adults 18 to 49, falling behind “American Idol” on Fox. According to Nielsen’s estimates, “The Office” drew approximately 8.3 million viewers from 9 to 9:53 p.m., ending just short of the hour and the start of an extended version of “Parks and Recreation” (4.6 million). Although ratings for “The Office” were the highest since January, NBC still lagged behind the other networks. It was a distant fourth place for the night in total viewers, garnering just 4 million for “30 Rock” at 10:30 p.m. and 3.6 million for “Community” at 8.

headline.main: ‘The Office’ Helps NBC, but Can’t Save It

docs.snippet: Some 20 years after the musical heyday of this English city, a wave of new clubs and venues is trading on “Madchester” nostalgia.
docs.lead_paragraph: A COUPLE of decades ago, if you were visiting Manchester you were probably there for business, or perhaps because of familial commitments. But while staggering unemployment and urban decay didn’t inspire much in the way of tourism to this post-industrial English city, it did inspire a movement of disaffected youth whose music still resonates. Indeed, while the grim years that inspired the depressive romanticism of bands like Joy Division and the Smiths have made way for large-scale urban development, Manchester’s prolific musical energy hasn’t dissipated.

docs.snippet: Daniel Rose’s 29-seat Spring restaurant, after its move from the Ninth to the First Arrondissement, still books up months in advance, and for good reason.
docs.lead_paragraph: For a while there, Daniel Rose had a pretty sweet gig. Spring, the young Chicago-born chef’s restaurant in the Ninth Arrondissement of Paris, was booked months in advance. A darling of the press, he was also the dauphin of his tiny open kitchen, which allowed him to chat with his 16 diners as he prepared the market-driven menu on his own slightly disorganized time. Your appetizer might have landed around bedtime, but you felt lucky to be there. (And you were.)

headline.main: Restaurant Review: Spring Restaurant, in Paris

docs.abstract: On Italy’s northeastern shore, Trieste doesn’t preen for tourists. Yet it is possessed of an odd magic, one that echoes its literary past.
docs.snippet: On Italy’s northeastern shore, Trieste doesn’t preen for tourists. Yet it is possessed of an odd magic, one that echoes its literary past.
docs.lead_paragraph: A MEDIUM-SIZE seaport teetering on the edge of what we recognize as Italy, Trieste is a mysterious and puzzling place. Its iconic central square, the Piazza dell’Unità d’Italia, bounded on three sides by comically pompous 18th- and 19th-century buildings, most of them decorated like big, boxy wedding cakes, is wide open to the Adriatic, as though the ever-changing seascape were an entertainment staged for the city’s benefit. This vast, glorious piazza promises all sorts of civic delights, but in fact it’s one of the few immediately gratifying spots in Trieste. The rest takes time — exactly what most of us are unwilling to give up.

headline.main: In a Quiet Corner of Italy ... Trieste
headline.print_headline: The Quiet One

docs.abstract: In the 1960s, when California still seemed like a paradise of leisure, it spawned a series of awful beach-party movies.
docs.snippet: In the 1960s, when California still seemed like a paradise of leisure, it spawned a series of awful beach-party movies.
docs.lead_paragraph: CALIFORNIA has fallen on grim economic times, but there was a period not long ago when, in popular culture at least, the Golden State seemed like the best idea America had ever had. In the 1950s and ’60s, even with the Gold Rush a century past, California still had its sand and its sun and its surf to beckon the hopeful westward, and of course it had the movies too, on screens as big — and sometimes as loud — as giant waves. After the gloom and horror of the Second World War and in the midst of the cold war’s nagging anxieties, all those bright blue skies and that warm Pacific water and that clean, soft, shimmery sand looked mighty inviting. “Catch a wave,” the Beach Boys sang, “and you’re be sittin’ on top of the world.” They sounded as if they meant it.

headline.main: Oh, Kahuna, What Became of That Endless Summer?

docs.abstract: We asked Anthony Tommasini, the  chief classical music critic of The Times, who interviewed Ms. Rice about her chamber music experience in a profile in 2005, to identify the pieces.
docs.snippet: We asked Anthony Tommasini, the  chief classical music critic of The Times, who interviewed Ms. Rice about her chamber music experience in a profile in 2005, to identify the pieces.
docs.lead_paragraph: Of the many bizarre plot lines running through last night’s episode of “30 Rock,” Condoleezza Rice’s sly cameo as the ex-girlfriend of Alec Baldwin’s character, Jack Donaghy, was by far the highlight. In the scene, shown above, Ms. Rice, a former secretary of state and classically trained pianist, challenged Mr. Baldwin, a Lincoln Center regular himself, to a musical face-off. (Mr. Baldwin does not actually perform in the episode.) We asked Anthony Tommasini, the chief classical music critic of The Times, who interviewed Ms. Rice about her chamber music experience in a profile in 2005, to identify the pieces. “They are all by Mozart,” he said. “The first is the opening of the third movement, the Rondo, from the Piano Quartet in G minor. The second is the opening of the first movement, the Allegro, of that same Piano Quartet in G minor. The third, and this gets complicated, is the slow movement, the Romanze, of the Piano Concerto No. 20 in D minor, not the opening of the movement, but the beginning of the fast middle section of that movement. Whew.” For insiders, Mr. Tommasini said, “the joke is the snippets of pieces played are not at all pieces for flute.” He added, “He tried to match her playing this music on the solo flute, an unfair match.”

headline.main: What Was Condoleezza Rice Playing on ’30 Rock’?

docs.abstract: The interconnected episodes of “Family Guy,” “The Cleveland Show” and “American Dad” were planned several months ago, before the recent storms that have killed nearly 300 people in the South.
docs.snippet: The interconnected episodes of “Family Guy,” “The Cleveland Show” and “American Dad” were planned several months ago, before the recent storms that have killed nearly 300 people in the South.
docs.lead_paragraph: Though the animated Fox comedies “Family Guy,” “The Cleveland Show” and “American Dad” are occasionally known for courting controversy, the network has decided to hold off on broadcasting episodes of those shows that were too close to current events for comfort. Fox was planning on Sunday to show new installments of those series with an interconnected story line about a hurricane on the Eastern Seaboard. These episodes were planned several months ago, before the recent storms that have killed nearly 300 people in the South. But on Friday, Fox said in a brief statement, “In light of the recent storms that have affected the nation, Fox has decided to postpone the crossover episodes of ‘Family Guy,’ ‘American Dad’ and ‘The Cleveland Show’ that were originally scheduled to air this Sunday.” A spokeswoman for the network said these episodes will instead be shown next season.

headline.main: Fox Postpones Animated Comedies With Hurricane Story Line

docs.abstract: A pop-up tattoo parlor created for Berlin’s Gallery Weekend demands a whole other level of commitment from prospective art buyers.
docs.snippet: A pop-up tattoo parlor created for Berlin’s Gallery Weekend demands a whole other level of commitment from prospective art buyers.
docs.lead_paragraph: Building a first-class art collection takes a lot of time and a lot of money, but the latest show at the Berlin gallery Arratia Beer, “As Long As It Lasts…,” demands a whole other level of commitment from its prospective buyers. The curators, Josée Lepage and Aric Chen (who has written for The Times), and the gallery have created a pop-up tattoo parlor, engaging one of the city’s best tattoo artists, Sarah Bolen from AKA Berlin, and offering designs from a diverse group of artists and designers, including heavyweights like Lawrence Weiner and Wim Delvoye, as well as fashion favorites like the architect Peter Marino and the German conceptual pranksters Bless. One of the most compelling designs comes courtesy of Olaf Nicolai, who suggests that collectors mark the initials of someone they love or hate using his codified variation on the alphabet. In designing his alphabet, Nicolai says that he “found [a] minimalistic style more interesting,” which didn’t function “like a billboard.” (In other words, you’re out of luck if you’re looking for hearts pierced by daggers or busty mermaids.) His design emphasizes “not just information, but also communication. You have to ask the person [what the tattoo means] if you want to understand it.”

docs.lead_paragraph: Andrew Morton, who has written biographies of Diana, Princess of Wales, Monica Lewinsky and Tom Cruise, has turned to a familiar subject for his next book: the newly wedded royal couple Prince William and the former Kate Middleton. St. Martin’s Press said on Friday that it would publish “William & Catherine: Their Story” on May 17, promising that Mr. Morton will tell “the full story” of the couple, including their time at university together, the prince’s proposal in Kenya and the wedding itself, with all its pomp and circumstance. “I have drawn on 30 years of experience covering the royal family to bring perspective and insight into the life of a young man I have watched develop from a toddler and schoolboy into a soldier — just as I have tried to discover more about his bride,” Mr. Morton said in a statement. The book is not an authorized biography, however, and Mr. Morton did not interview William or the Duchess of Cambridge, as she is now known.

headline.main: Biography of Royal Newlyweds Due May 17

docs.lead_paragraph: The summer issue of T Design and Living is all about visions of home. For the high-powered money manager in “Embassy Suite,” being the wife of the American ambassador to France gives new meaning to the phrase “gracious living.” T also visits the young designers Big-Game and Formafantasma; the art director Sofía Sanchez Barrenechea; Ai-Jen Poo, a crusader for domestic workers’ rights; and stylish stops in Turin, Italy. And the Edible Selby samples the java at Blue Bottle. See more from the issue >>

docs.abstract: How to annotate your digital copies of books when using the iPad.
docs.snippet: How to annotate your digital copies of books when using the iPad.
docs.lead_paragraph: Like other e-book readers, the iBooks app for the iPad (and iPhone or iPod Touch) allows you to make margin notes inside digital books. To make a note in an open iBooks file, press down on the iPad’s screen to select the word or phrase you want to annotate. In the menu bar that appears above your selected text, tap the Note button to create a digital sticky note and use the iPad keyboard to type in your thoughts. When you tap the text behind the note, the note file shrinks to a small square on the edge of the book’s page, near the highlighted text you originally selected. Tap the shrunken note to expand it so you can review your annotations.

headline.main: Tip of the Week: Making Notes in iBooks

docs.lead_paragraph: HAVEN is one of a handful of restaurants that have responded enthusiastically to a growing demand for seasonal offerings that are healthful, creative and reasonably priced. Judging by weekend crowds especially, Daniel Petrilli, the owner and chef of this Pleasantville dining spot, has been successful in giving diners what they want.
